TARGETED TEMPERATURE MANAGEMENT AFTER CARDIAC ARREST
Rationale: Fever is associated with worse neurological outcomes and neuronal damage due to inflammatory changes and biochemical
cascades that develop following ischemia and reperfusion injury associated with cardiac arrest (Arch Intern Med 2001). TTM is a class I
recommendation for all patients not following commands post arrest (AHA 2023). Goal is to avoid fever for neuroprotection and to be
aggressive about diagnosing/treating infections.
Causes of fever: Inflammatory response to global ischemia-reperfusion, drug fever, and/or infection
• High infection risk in all post arrest patients from aspiration/pneumonia, global ischemia -> gut ischemia -> bacterial
translocation. Pan-culture and consider empiric antibiotic treatment.
• If on temperature control device preventing rise in temperature, potential fevers will present as changes in cooling pattern
*
)
TTM options if patient is not following commands (patient needs to be stable enough to wean sedation and paralysis for this exam):
• Normothermia (≤37.5 C)
o Allow passive rewarming until patient achieves T 37 C. Once at 37 C, use temp control device
o Arctic Sun or other temperature control device to maintain T <37.5 C for 72 hr
• Mild Hypothermia (T 33-36 C)
o Individualized patient selection for mild hypothermia (T 33-36 C) decided by primary team and Neurology
o Temperature control device placed as soon as possible with goal of achieving target temp within 4h of ROSC
o Maintain mild hypothermia for 24 hr, followed by normothermia for 48hr for total 72 hr
o For mild hypothermia, re-warming should occur at a target rate of 0.25 °C/h until normothermia achieved.
o Monitor blood glucose/electrolytes closely
o Relative Contraindications to Mild Hypothermia: Refractory hypotension, Recent head trauma, active bleeding, major
surgery (<14d)
Evidence:
-Targeted hypothermia (T 33 C) did not reduce 6-month mortality or survival with good neurologic outcome compared to targeted
normothermia (T<37.5 C) (NEJM 2021;384:2283)
-Whether certain subgroups benefit from targeted hypothermia is uncertain (e.g., initial non-shockable rhythm (NEJM 2019;381:2327))
-Currently insufficient evidence to recommend different therapeutic temperatures for specific cardiac arrest groups (Class 2b, AHA 2023)
Sedation and Analgesia:
-Patients should undergo continuous sedation/analgesia if undergoing TTM w/mild hypothermia. Propofol is preferred sedative agent,
dilaudid (or fentanyl) is preferred analgesic
Shivering:
-Stepwise approach to shivering in pts undergoing TTM (1st line: PR/PO acetaminophen 650q6 → IV, Mg >3, 2nd line: skin
counterwarming + dexmedetomidine OR propofol OR hydromorphone boluses, 3rd line: propofol + hydromorphone gtt, consider buspirone
30q8, 4th line: NMBA) (Neurocrit Care 2011;14:389)
Neuro-prognostication see Neurology section
Brian Huang

EXTERNAL DEFIBRILLATION/CARDIOVERSION/TRANSCUTANEOUS PACING
• About the device: . This device allows for external defibrillation, cardioversion, and
pacing with additional benefits (e.g. display ET-CO2, CPR quality feedback, & upload rhythm strips into Epic)
• Additional supplies/resources: Ambu bag, intubation equipment, , backboard, suction, LUCAS (cardiopulm assist system)
Medications: use procedural sedation (typically 50mcg fentanyl  2mg midazolam) when possible, .
In emergent situations, Dilaudid 1-2mg + lorazepam 2mg is a reasonable alternative (often readily available).

topics.title: EKG Interpretation

panels.title: Source content
panels.text:
Approach all EKGs systematically. Note rate, rhythm, QRS axis, intervals, complexes, chambers, ischemia/infarction. Compare with prior EKG.
RATE (atrial, ventricular)
• If regular, 300 / #large boxes between each QRS (60,000/rate = R-R interval in ms)
• If irregular, count # of QRSs on EKG and multiply by 6 (printout = 10 sec)
• Normal atrial rate 60-100bpm; <60 = bradycardia, >100 = tachycardia
o 100-180: sinus tachycardia; 140-220: atrial tachycardias, AVNRT/AVRT; 260-320: flutter
1 small box = 40 ms

panels.title: RHYTHM (regular or irregular; sinus vs non-sinus)
panels.text:
RHYTHM (regular or irregular; sinus vs non-sinus)
• Sinus rhythm = P before every QRS and QRS following every P, regular w/ rate 60-100, normal P wave axis
• P wave morphology: Is P wave present (best leads to visualize P wave are II and V1) and P wave axis (Normal: upright in I/II, biphasic in V1)
• QRS morphology: narrow (<120 ms) = supraventricular origin; wide (>120 ms) = aberrant supraventricular conduction or ventricular origin
• P wave/QRS complex association: if not 1:1: see if P>QRS (AV block) or P<QRS (AV node, His-Purkinje, or ventricular rhythm). If P precedes QRS,
evaluate PR interval. If P after QRS, evaluate RP interval. Determine if PR or RP interval is fixed or variable.
o AVB: first degree (PR >200ms); second degree Mobitz I/Wenckebach (PR progressively longer until dropped QRS); second degree Mobitz
type II (sudden dropped QRS without PR lengthening); third degree/complete heart block (dissociation of P and QRS)
QRS AXIS (use direction of QRS complex)
Axis Deviation Lead I Lead II Lead aVF Differential Diagnosis
Normal (-30 to +90º)   /-
Normal variant, mechanical shifts, LVH, LBBB, LAFB,
Leftward
 - - congenital heart disease, emphysema, hyperK,
(-30 to -90º)
ventricular ectopic rhythms, WPW, inferior MI, pacing
Normal variant, mechanical shifts, RV strain, RVH,
Rightward
-   LPFB, dextrocardia, ventricular ectopic rhythms,
(+90 to +180º)
WPW, lateral MI (RBBB rarely causes RAD)
Extreme/Northwest Lead transposition, ventricular ectopic rhythms,
- - -
(180 to -90º) hyperK, artificial pacing, severe RVH
• Clockwise/counterclockwise rotation (“R wave progression”): R wave amplitude typically increases from V1 to V5, amplitude of R becomes greater
than S at V3 or V4. Early or late R wave progression is nonspecific and can be normal (Am Heart J 2004;148:80)
o CCW (“early R wave progression”): R>S prior to V3. Causes: RVH, WPW, LAFB, posterior MI.
o CW (“late R wave progression”): R>S after V4. Causes: cardiomyopathy, LVH, LBBB, anterior MI.
• Low voltage: average QRS amplitude <5 mm in I, II, III and <10 mm in precordial leads
o DDx: obesity, pericardial effusion, PTX, COPD, PE, restrictive or infiltrative CM (particularly amyloidosis), severe hypothyroidism, or anasarca

panels.title: COMPLEXES AND INTERVALS (Circ 2009;119:e241)
panels.text:
COMPLEXES AND INTERVALS (Circ 2009;119:e241)
• P wave: right and left atrial depolarization. Normal: duration <120ms, voltage ≥ 0.1mV in I, area (1/2 duration x voltage in II) ≤ 4 (Circ Arrhythm
Electrophysiol. 2022; e010435)
• PR interval: atrial depolarization, AV node and His-Purkinje conduction. Normally 140-200ms, changes with rate (shortened at faster rates, longer at
lower rates) d/t autonomic effects on AV nodal conduction
• QRS: ventricular depolarization. Normal duration 60-110ms, not influenced by HR. QRS 100-120ms = incomplete BBB or intraventricular conduction
delay (IVCD). QRS >120ms = BBB, ventricular activation (PVC, VT, fusion beats, WPW, paced beats), hyperK, Na channel poisoning, aberrancy,
hypothermia.

panels.title: ST SEGMENT AND T WAVE CHANGES (JACC 2009;53:1003)
panels.text:
ST SEGMENT AND T WAVE CHANGES (JACC 2009;53:1003)
• Analyze abnormalities along the vectors of ventricular depolarization and repolarization (QRS-ST-T)
• T wave abnormalities: hyperacute, symmetric T waves can be found within minutes of ischemia, followed by T wave inversions (≥1mm in 2
contiguous leads). TWI normal if only in aVR, V1 or III. Isolated TWI in aVL may indicate mid-LAD lesion vs inferior MI (J Emerg Med 2014;46:165)
o TWI DDx: myocardial ischemia (symmetric), prior MI, acute PE (RV strain pattern: TWI V1-V4, II, III, aVF, RBBB, ↑Sp/↓Sn: S1Q3T3, TWI
III+V1 high PPV for PE > ACS (Am J Card 2007;99:817)), apical HCM (TWI V1-V6), arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (TWI V1-
3), intracranial pathology (“cerebral T waves”, asymmetric), myocarditis, pericarditis, BBB pattern, V-paced, LVH with “strain”, normal variant,
digoxin effect (biphasic w/ initial neg. predominance), Type 1 Brugada (TWI V1-V2), athlete’s heart. (World J Cardiol. 2015; 7(2): 86-100).
o De Winter’s T waves: 2% of STEMIs present with tall, symmetric T waves + >1mm STD at J point in precordial leads + 0.5-1mm STE in aVR
c/w acute LAD occlusion (NEJM 2008;359:2071)
• ST depression: suggests subendocardial injury, ≥0.5mm below the baseline (TP segment), measured 80ms after the J point in 2 contiguous leads
o Downsloping or horizontal = more ominous. STD in isolation do not localize ischemia to a specific territory (Circ Res 1998;82;957)
o Always look for STE to rule out reciprocal STD. STD in V1-V3 can be posterior MI (check posterior leads)
• ST elevation: suggests transmural ischemia, ≥1mm in leads except for leads V2-V3 (≥2mm in M ≥40y, ≥2.5mm in M ≤40y, ≥1.5mm in F),
measured at the J point, use TP segment (isoelectric interval) as baseline (Circ 2018: e618-e651). Differential diagnosis:
Diagnosis w/ STE Characteristic ECG Findings (NEJM 2003;349:2128; Annals 2004;141:858; NEJM 2004;351:2195)
Acute STEMI STE in ≥2 contiguous leads in coronary distribution (see table), reciprocal STD
LVH Concave STE in V1-V3 with STD and TWI in I, aVL, V5-V6, voltage criteria as above
LBBB Concave STE in V1-V3, discordant with negative QRS
Acute pericarditis Diffuse STE (usually <5mm), PR depression, amplitude of STE:T wave (in mm) >0.26 is specific
Printzmetal’s angina/vasospasm Transient STE in coronary distribution as in STEMI
Acute PE STE in inferior and anteroseptal leads, mimics acute MI, complete or incomplete RBBB
Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo’s) Diffuse STE in precordial leads w/o reciprocal inferior STD, STE followed by deep TWI
Ventricular aneurysm Persistent STE after MI, often with abnormal Q waves
Early repolarization J point elevation ≥1mm in 2 contiguous leads (esp V4), amplitude of STE:T wave (in mm) <0.25
Brugada syndrome rSR’ and downsloping STE in V1-V2 (see below)
Male pattern 1-3mm concave STE, often highest in V2
Normal variant STE in V3-V5, TWI, short QT, high QRS voltage
Cardioversion Marked (often >10mm) and transient following DCCV
Coronary Distribution Modified Sgarbossa Criteria:
EKG Lead Territory Coronary Vessel To diagnose acute MI w/ LBBB
V1-V2 Anteroseptal Proximal-mid LAD (does not apply to pacers). Below =
V5-V6 Apical Distal LAD, Distal LCx, RCA traditional version (need 3pts)
I, aVL Lateral LCx (proximal) • Concordant STE >1mm in any
II, III, aVF Inferior RCA (85%), LCx lead = 5 points
V7-V9 Posterior LCx > RCA • Discordant STE >5mm in any
V4R RV RCA, LCx lead = 2 points
aVR L main or 3vD • STD >1mm in V1-V3 = 3 points
• Q wave: usually a marker of scar, pathologic Q waves must be deep (>1mm), 25% height of QRS, and 40ms Wellens Type A Wellens Type B
long. More likely 2/2 prior MI if inverted T wave in same lead. Small “septal” Q physiologic in V5, V6, I, aVL
• Wellens Syndrome: sign of critical proximal LM or LAD lesion, 75% MI in <2w. Often pain free with h/o
angina. Normal/slightly elevated troponin. Type A: 25% biphasic (up then downsloping morphology) T waves in
V2 and V3. Type B: 75% symmetric, deeply inverted precordial T waves. Isoelectric or minimally elevated
(<1mm) ST segment. No precordial Q waves (Am J Emerg Med 2002;20:7; Am Heart J 1982;103:730)

panels.title: OTHER
panels.text:
OTHER
• J-Point Elevation Syndromes: J point is when QRS transitions to ST segment. BER Brugada 1
o Benign early repolarization (BER): upsloping STE in young (<50), asymptomatic, healthy patients;
commonly w/ notched J joint. Has some associations with adverse outcomes but not well understood.
▪ Suspicious features: FH sudden cardiac arrest or early unexplained death, workup c/f
channelopathy, unheralded syncope c/f arrhythmogenic pathogenesis (Circ 2016;133:1520)
o Brugada Pattern: 3 different classic patterns (Brugada 1-3), brugada syndrome only if symptomatic.
Autosomal dominant SCN5A loss of function in 10-30%, M>F, nocturnal cardiac arrest common, p/w
VT/VF or sudden cardiac death (Circ Arrhythm Electrophys 2012;5:606)
• Osborn wave: hypothermia T<93ºF, occurs before J point, can cause elevation of J point height ~ Osborn wave Delta wave
proportional to degree of hypothermia in II, V2-6. More dome-shaped than Epsilon wave.
• Delta wave: slurred upstroke of QRS indicative of pre-excitation. Found in Wolff Parkinson’s White
syndrome with a short PR interval and a prolonged QRS complex
• Epsilon wave: Low frequency, positive terminal deflection in V1-V3. Found in arrhythmogenic right
ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) (Circ 2005;112:3823), most Sp in V1 (30% with ARVC)
• Electrolyte Abnormalities:
Abnormality Characteristic ECG Findings
Hypokalemia Prolonged QT, ST depression, flattened T wave, prominent U wave, higher amplitude P wave, prolonged PR
Hyperkalemia Peaked, symmetric T wave → flat P → prolonged PR ± AVB → widened QRS ± BBB (severe) → sinusoidal
Hypocalcemia Prolonged QT, unchanged T wave
Hypercalcemia Shortened QT (if severe, T-wave can merge with QRS and mimic STE)

topics.text:
Cardiology EKG Interpretation
Approach all EKGs systematically. Note rate, rhythm, QRS axis, intervals, complexes, chambers, ischemia/infarction. Compare with prior EKG.
RATE (atrial, ventricular)
• If regular, 300 / #large boxes between each QRS (60,000/rate = R-R interval in ms)
• If irregular, count # of QRSs on EKG and multiply by 6 (printout = 10 sec)
• Normal atrial rate 60-100bpm; <60 = bradycardia, >100 = tachycardia
o 100-180: sinus tachycardia; 140-220: atrial tachycardias, AVNRT/AVRT; 260-320: flutter
1 small box = 40 ms
RHYTHM (regular or irregular; sinus vs non-sinus)
• Sinus rhythm = P before every QRS and QRS following every P, regular w/ rate 60-100, normal P wave axis
• P wave morphology: Is P wave present (best leads to visualize P wave are II and V1) and P wave axis (Normal: upright in I/II, biphasic in V1)
• QRS morphology: narrow (<120 ms) = supraventricular origin; wide (>120 ms) = aberrant supraventricular conduction or ventricular origin
• P wave/QRS complex association: if not 1:1: see if P>QRS (AV block) or P<QRS (AV node, His-Purkinje, or ventricular rhythm). If P precedes QRS,
evaluate PR interval. If P after QRS, evaluate RP interval. Determine if PR or RP interval is fixed or variable.
o AVB: first degree (PR >200ms); second degree Mobitz I/Wenckebach (PR progressively longer until dropped QRS); second degree Mobitz
type II (sudden dropped QRS without PR lengthening); third degree/complete heart block (dissociation of P and QRS)
QRS AXIS (use direction of QRS complex)
Axis Deviation Lead I Lead II Lead aVF Differential Diagnosis
Normal (-30 to +90º)   /-

(180 to -90º) hyperK, artificial pacing, severe RVH
• Clockwise/counterclockwise rotation (“R wave progression”): R wave amplitude typically increases from V1 to V5, amplitude of R becomes greater
than S at V3 or V4. Early or late R wave progression is nonspecific and can be normal (Am Heart J 2004;148:80)
o CCW (“early R wave progression”): R>S prior to V3. Causes: RVH, WPW, LAFB, posterior MI.
o CW (“late R wave progression”): R>S after V4. Causes: cardiomyopathy, LVH, LBBB, anterior MI.
• Low voltage: average QRS amplitude <5 mm in I, II, III and <10 mm in precordial leads
o DDx: obesity, pericardial effusion, PTX, COPD, PE, restrictive or infiltrative CM (particularly amyloidosis), severe hypothyroidism, or anasarca
COMPLEXES AND INTERVALS (Circ 2009;119:e241)
• P wave: right and left atrial depolarization. Normal: duration <120ms, voltage ≥ 0.1mV in I, area (1/2 duration x voltage in II) ≤ 4 (Circ Arrhythm
Electrophysiol. 2022; e010435)
• PR interval: atrial depolarization, AV node and His-Purkinje conduction. Normally 140-200ms, changes with rate (shortened at faster rates, longer at
lower rates) d/t autonomic effects on AV nodal conduction
• QRS: ventricular depolarization. Normal duration 60-110ms, not influenced by HR. QRS 100-120ms = incomplete BBB or intraventricular conduction
delay (IVCD). QRS >120ms = BBB, ventricular activation (PVC, VT, fusion beats, WPW, paced beats), hyperK, Na channel poisoning, aberrancy,
hypothermia.

Cardiology EKG Interpretation
• RAE: P wave height >2.5mm in II (“P-pulmonae”), initial positive P wave in V1/V2 ≥1.5mm
ST SEGMENT AND T WAVE CHANGES (JACC 2009;53:1003)
• Analyze abnormalities along the vectors of ventricular depolarization and repolarization (QRS-ST-T)
• T wave abnormalities: hyperacute, symmetric T waves can be found within minutes of ischemia, followed by T wave inversions (≥1mm in 2
contiguous leads). TWI normal if only in aVR, V1 or III. Isolated TWI in aVL may indicate mid-LAD lesion vs inferior MI (J Emerg Med 2014;46:165)
o TWI DDx: myocardial ischemia (symmetric), prior MI, acute PE (RV strain pattern: TWI V1-V4, II, III, aVF, RBBB, ↑Sp/↓Sn: S1Q3T3, TWI
III+V1 high PPV for PE > ACS (Am J Card 2007;99:817)), apical HCM (TWI V1-V6), arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (TWI V1-
3), intracranial pathology (“cerebral T waves”, asymmetric), myocarditis, pericarditis, BBB pattern, V-paced, LVH with “strain”, normal variant,
digoxin effect (biphasic w/ initial neg. predominance), Type 1 Brugada (TWI V1-V2), athlete’s heart. (World J Cardiol. 2015; 7(2): 86-100).
o De Winter’s T waves: 2% of STEMIs present with tall, symmetric T waves + >1mm STD at J point in precordial leads + 0.5-1mm STE in aVR
c/w acute LAD occlusion (NEJM 2008;359:2071)
• ST depression: suggests subendocardial injury, ≥0.5mm below the baseline (TP segment), measured 80ms after the J point in 2 contiguous leads
o Downsloping or horizontal = more ominous. STD in isolation do not localize ischemia to a specific territory (Circ Res 1998;82;957)
o Always look for STE to rule out reciprocal STD. STD in V1-V3 can be posterior MI (check posterior leads)
• ST elevation: suggests transmural ischemia, ≥1mm in leads except for leads V2-V3 (≥2mm in M ≥40y, ≥2.5mm in M ≤40y, ≥1.5mm in F),
measured at the J point, use TP segment (isoelectric interval) as baseline (Circ 2018: e618-e651). Differential diagnosis:
Diagnosis w/ STE Characteristic ECG Findings (NEJM 2003;349:2128; Annals 2004;141:858; NEJM 2004;351:2195)
Acute STEMI STE in ≥2 contiguous leads in coronary distribution (see table), reciprocal STD
LVH Concave STE in V1-V3 with STD and TWI in I, aVL, V5-V6, voltage criteria as above
LBBB Concave STE in V1-V3, discordant with negative QRS
Acute pericarditis Diffuse STE (usually <5mm), PR depression, amplitude of STE:T wave (in mm) >0.26 is specific
Printzmetal’s angina/vasospasm Transient STE in coronary distribution as in STEMI
Acute PE STE in inferior and anteroseptal leads, mimics acute MI, complete or incomplete RBBB
Stress-induced cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo’s) Diffuse STE in precordial leads w/o reciprocal inferior STD, STE followed by deep TWI
Ventricular aneurysm Persistent STE after MI, often with abnormal Q waves
Early repolarization J point elevation ≥1mm in 2 contiguous leads (esp V4), amplitude of STE:T wave (in mm) <0.25
Brugada syndrome rSR’ and downsloping STE in V1-V2 (see below)
Male pattern 1-3mm concave STE, often highest in V2
Normal variant STE in V3-V5, TWI, short QT, high QRS voltage
Cardioversion Marked (often >10mm) and transient following DCCV
Coronary Distribution Modified Sgarbossa Criteria:
EKG Lead Territory Coronary Vessel To diagnose acute MI w/ LBBB
V1-V2 Anteroseptal Proximal-mid LAD (does not apply to pacers). Below =
V5-V6 Apical Distal LAD, Distal LCx, RCA traditional version (need 3pts)
I, aVL Lateral LCx (proximal) • Concordant STE >1mm in any
II, III, aVF Inferior RCA (85%), LCx lead = 5 points
V7-V9 Posterior LCx > RCA • Discordant STE >5mm in any
V4R RV RCA, LCx lead = 2 points
aVR L main or 3vD • STD >1mm in V1-V3 = 3 points
• Q wave: usually a marker of scar, pathologic Q waves must be deep (>1mm), 25% height of QRS, and 40ms Wellens Type A Wellens Type B
long. More likely 2/2 prior MI if inverted T wave in same lead. Small “septal” Q physiologic in V5, V6, I, aVL
• Wellens Syndrome: sign of critical proximal LM or LAD lesion, 75% MI in <2w. Often pain free with h/o
angina. Normal/slightly elevated troponin. Type A: 25% biphasic (up then downsloping morphology) T waves in
V2 and V3. Type B: 75% symmetric, deeply inverted precordial T waves. Isoelectric or minimally elevated
(<1mm) ST segment. No precordial Q waves (Am J Emerg Med 2002;20:7; Am Heart J 1982;103:730)
OTHER
• J-Point Elevation Syndromes: J point is when QRS transitions to ST segment. BER Brugada 1
o Benign early repolarization (BER): upsloping STE in young (<50), asymptomatic, healthy patients;
commonly w/ notched J joint. Has some associations with adverse outcomes but not well understood.
▪ Suspicious features: FH sudden cardiac arrest or early unexplained death, workup c/f
channelopathy, unheralded syncope c/f arrhythmogenic pathogenesis (Circ 2016;133:1520)
o Brugada Pattern: 3 different classic patterns (Brugada 1-3), brugada syndrome only if symptomatic.
Autosomal dominant SCN5A loss of function in 10-30%, M>F, nocturnal cardiac arrest common, p/w
VT/VF or sudden cardiac death (Circ Arrhythm Electrophys 2012;5:606)
• Osborn wave: hypothermia T<93ºF, occurs before J point, can cause elevation of J point height ~ Osborn wave Delta wave
proportional to degree of hypothermia in II, V2-6. More dome-shaped than Epsilon wave.
• Delta wave: slurred upstroke of QRS indicative of pre-excitation. Found in Wolff Parkinson’s White
syndrome with a short PR interval and a prolonged QRS complex
• Epsilon wave: Low frequency, positive terminal deflection in V1-V3. Found in arrhythmogenic right
ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) (Circ 2005;112:3823), most Sp in V1 (30% with ARVC)
• Electrolyte Abnormalities:
Abnormality Characteristic ECG Findings
Hypokalemia Prolonged QT, ST depression, flattened T wave, prominent U wave, higher amplitude P wave, prolonged PR
Hyperkalemia Peaked, symmetric T wave → flat P → prolonged PR ± AVB → widened QRS ± BBB (severe) → sinusoidal
Hypocalcemia Prolonged QT, unchanged T wave
Hypercalcemia Shortened QT (if severe, T-wave can merge with QRS and mimic STE)

topics.title: Wide Complex Tachycardia

panels.title: WIDE COMPLEX TACHYCARDIA (QRS ≥120MS)
panels.text:
WIDE COMPLEX TACHYCARDIA (QRS ≥120MS)
DDx = VT (80%), SVT with aberrant conduction, pre-excitation syndrome, or pacemaker-mediated tachycardia
Features that Favor VT (note: absence does NOT rule out VT) Features that Favor SVT with Aberrancy
• History of structural heart disease, prior MI, ICD • Known BBB: ventricular conduction delay
• Very wide QRS (>160 ms), Rate > 120 (if <120, consider Na channel (RBBB, LBBB, IVCD) with similar morphology
toxicity or VT in someone already on significant antiarrhythmics) and axis as seen on prior / baseline ECG
• New northwest (aka extreme) axis (leads I and II negative) • Evidence of His conduction: QRS has sharp
• AV dissociation (often V rate > A rate): pathognomonic for VT initial deflection (suggests initial use of His-
• Concordance: all QRS in V1-6 are completely (+) or completely (-) Purkinje system followed by aberrancy)
• Partial (fusion beat) or complete (capture beat) depolarization of His- • Pre-excitation on baseline ECG  supports
Purkinje by a competing supraventricular (atrial / junctional) rhythm antidromic AVRT or pre-excited atrial fibrillation
• Basel algorithm = VT likely if ≥2 of 3 present: (1) high risk substrate (prior • R wave peak time < 40msec (measured in lead
MI, EF<35, prior VT/has ICD), (2) lead II time to first peak >40ms (1 small II and aVR)
box), (3) aVR time to first peak >40ms (1 small box).
▪ Very effective: 93% sensitive & 90% specific (JACC 2022;7:831).
• Brugada algorithm also commonly utilized – see below.
Other important considerations:
• Hyperkalemia, antiarrhythmic drugs (digoxin, class IA or IC, amiodarone), TCA overdose
• Pacemaker-mediated/endless loop ta chycardia: retrograde VA conduction of V-paced beat misidentified as native A-beat  V-
pacing. ECG shows V pacing at upper rate limit
• Sensor induced tachycardia: inappropriate sensing of nonphysi ologic stimuli (vibrations, electrocautery, etc.) and pacing.

panels.title: MANAGEMENT OF VT (also see ACLS: Tachycardia)
panels.text:
MANAGEMENT OF VT (also see ACLS: Tachycardia)
• Often no way to confidently distinguish VT vs SVT with aberrancy. If there is any doubt, treat like VT
• Consider underlying processes: active ischemia, CAD with scar, electrolyte derangement (low K, low Mg), drug toxicity, indwelling
lines, thyrotoxicosis
• Check and replenish electrolytes (K>4, Mg>2)
• Review baseline ECG for evidence of long QT or pre-excitation
Monomorphic VT Polymorphic VT
Torsades de Pointes
DDx: ischemia, structural heart disease, idiopathic DDx: ischemia (ac ute, CAD, ICM) vs. prolonged QTc
Non-sustained VT (>3 complexes, <30 secs): Unstable  defibrillation Polymorphic VT that occurs
Asymptomatic: monitor, treat underlying cardiac Baseline norm al QTc: emergent eval for with underlying prolonged
comorbidities (e.g., CAD, HF) revasc (ische mia until proven otherwise), QTc (congenital or acquired).
Symptomatic or very high burden: nodal blockade AADs (amio, p rocainamide) Can be prompted by PVC
(BB>CCB), then AADs Baseline prolo nged QTc: magnesium 2-4g falling on T wave of previous
Stable and sustained (>30 seconds): antiarrhythmic over 10-15min , HR (isoproterenol, overdrive beat (R on T phenomenon)
agent (e.g. amiodarone, lidocaine, procainamide [WPW]) pacing), QTc (lido), avoid bradycardia (no Note: isoproterenol = pure
Unstable  synchronized cardioversion (100J) if pulse; amio, CCB/BB) chronotrope will reduce RoT
defibrillation if pulseless
VT Storm: ≥3 sustained episodes of unstable VT within 24 hours
• Call EP +/- MCS Shock Team
• Lido bolus (preferred if prolonged QTc), Amio bolus (careful if long QT), consider co-admin propranolol 40mg q6 (esp. if s/p
multiple defibrillations) [JACC 2018;71:1897]
• Anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP): overdrive pacing at a faster rate than VT
• Treat / minimize ischemia: urgent revascularization, IABP to improve coronary perfusion, reduce preload / afterload
• Reduce autonomic tone: intubation and sedation, stellate ganglion block/cardiac sympathetic denervation
• Catheter ablation: In refractory cases, some evidence for ablation first strategy in ischemic CM (VANISH trial, VANISH2 trial)

• Consider AF burden when estimating stroke risk (JAMA Card 2018;601). Subclinical AF is also associated w/ increased

• DOACs vs warfarin: DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) recommended > warfarin in all except valvular AF, mod-
severe mitral stenosis, HOCM, or mechanical valve. Warfarin may be > rivaroxaban in rheumatic heart dz (NEJM 2022;387:978).

• Renal impairment: for pts w/ CrCl<15 or on dialysis, can use either warfarin or apixaban

Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion (LAAO) - LAA is the source of at least 90% of thrombi in pts with CVA and AF

undergoing cardiac surgery in addition to continued AC (Circ 2024; 149: e1-e156).

• Traditionally, rate control considered noninferior to rhythm control for AF sx, CV mortality, & stroke risk (AFFIRM, RACE, PIAF, STAF,
HOT CAFÉ, AF-CHF). Latest guidelines shifted with benefit of early rhythm control and reducing AF burden. (Circ 2024; 149: e1-e156)
• Rhythm control (antiarrhythmics and AF ablation) superior to usual care (rate control) for patients with recently diagnosed AF (within
1 year) and concomitant CV conditions in decreasing CV mortality, stroke, and hospitalization for HF or ACS (EAST-AFNET 4)

o Restoration of NSR may lead to increased quality of life & exercise performance (NEJM 2005;352:1861; JACC 2004;43:241)

o BB > CCB in achieving rate control (70% vs 54%), either alone or in combination with digoxin
o Digoxin alone is moderately effective in controlling V-rate at rest (time to onset 3-6 hrs), ineffective w/ high adrenergic tone

1st line), cautious use in high-degree AVB. CCB should not be used in pts with LVEF <40% given negative inotropy

o Choice of Agents:
▪ No structural heart disease: flecainide,propafenone, dofetilide, dronedarone, sotalol, amiodarone
▪ Structural heart disease: CAD: dofetilide, dronedarone, sotalol, amiodarone; HF or LVH: amio, dofetilide
o “Pill-in-Pocket”: for patients with recent pAF and infrequent and well-tolerated episodes, ppx may have risk>benefit. PRN
flecainide or propafenone + BB or CCB instead at symptom onset is safe and effective (NEJM 2004;351:2384)

strategy (NEJM 2021;384:305)long-term AF recurrence rate vs AADs in both pAF (MANTRA-PAF) & persistent AF (EHJ
2014;35:501). Ablation in pts w/ HF morbidity/mortality (CASTLE-AF) and improves psychological distress. (JAMA 2023;330:925)
o AV nodal ablation with PPM: indicated when pharmacologic rate/rhythm control not achievable (JACC 2014;64:2246)

panels.title: ATRIAL FLUTTER (AFL, less prevalent but often coexists with or precedes AF)
panels.text:
ATRIAL FLUTTER (AFL, less prevalent but often coexists with or precedes AF)
• ECG: “sawtooth” P waves (F waves), atrial rate typically 250-300bpm w/ 2:1 conduction (~V-rate 150), though can be variable block,
3:1, or 4:1. 1:1 conduction can briefly precede VT/VF
o Type 1 (typical): reentrant loop in RA via cavo-tricuspid isthmus
▪ Counterclockwise: more common, inverted flutter waves II, III, aVF + upright flutter waves V1
▪ Clockwise: less common, upright flutter waves in II, III, aVF + inverted flutter waves in V1
o Type 2 (atypical): does not meet criteria for Type 1; is often faster and refractory to ablation
• Anticoagulation: risk of thromboembolism lower than AF (J Stroke Cerebrovasc 2018;27:839) but
anticoagulation management is similar to AF (Chest 2012;141:e531S)
• Rate control: similar strategies (BB, CCB) to AF, but more difficult to successfully rate-control vs. AF
• Rhythm control: Ablation > AAD. Cavo-tricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation for typical flutter >90%
effective at 1y (Circ Arrhythmia EP 2009;2:393). However, prophylactic CTI ablation during PVI for AF pts
without known AFL does not reduce incidence of AFL or recurrence of AF (Arryth EP Rev 2022; e10).
Yichi Zhang

topics.title: QTc Prolongation

panels.title: DEFINITION (Circ 2009; 119: e241)
panels.text:
DEFINITION (Circ 2009; 119: e241)
• QT interval correlates with repolarization time of ventricles
• Normal: ≤460ms; Borderline (adult): 460-479ms (female), 450-459ms (male)
• Measure from beginning of QRS to end of T wave in a lead with T wave > 2mm
(best in II, V5), define end point using tangent from peak of steepest slope to
isoelectric line; can use ECG or caliper function on telemetry
• QTc is QT corrected for HR; linear (i.e., Hodges/Framingham) formulas are
recommended by AHA (J Electrocardiology 2004;37:81)
• Can be calculated using MDCalc: Framingham and Fridericia provide best rate
correction and mortality prediction (JAHA 2016;5:e003264)

panels.title: ASSESSMENT OF QTC WITH UNDERLYING WIDE QRS (Heart Rhythm 2014;11:2273)
panels.text:
ASSESSMENT OF QTC WITH UNDERLYING WIDE QRS (Heart Rhythm 2014;11:2273)
• Wide QRS (BBB/V-paced) lengthens QT interval; calculate using Mayo calculator, or with rough estimate using QT - (0.5*QRS).
Must still account for HR (Heart Rhythm. 2014 Dec;11(12)).

panels.title: CONGENITAL LONG-QT SYNDROMES
panels.text:
CONGENITAL LONG-QT SYNDROMES
• Majority of pts are asymptomatic, often discovered on ECG or QTc prolonged more than should be expected by drugs
• Sx: presyncope/syncope, hemodynamic compromise, sudden cardiac death; triggered by exercise, stress
• Tx: beta blocker for all, ICD if previous cardiac arrest and expected survival >1y (Class 1A Recommendation) (Circ 2006;114:e385)
o BB thought to reduce early after-depolarizations and transmural dispersion of repolarizations, which can trigger arrhythmias

panels.title: DRUG-INDUCED PROLONGED QT INTERVAL (Heart 2003;89:1363; NEJM 2004;350:1013)
panels.text:
DRUG-INDUCED PROLONGED QT INTERVAL (Heart 2003;89:1363; NEJM 2004;350:1013)
• Drugs inhibit rapid K+ current causing prolonged ventricular repolarization & exaggerate heterogeneity in repolarization times in
different layers of myocardium leading to reentry and tachyarrhythmia
Danger of prolonged QT = increased risk of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), which can degenerate into VF
Longer QT increases risk for “R on T” phenomenon and development of TdP (higher risk if PVCs)

panels.title: MONITORING FOR QT/QTC PROLONGATION
panels.text:
MONITORING FOR QT/QTC PROLONGATION
• Check QTc before and 12h after initiation/increased dose of QT-prolonging drug. Continue monitoring if prolongation is seen.
o Check QTc 2h post loading-dose of sotalol or dofetilide R on T
• Class I indications for QTc monitoring with ECG (Circ 2004;110:2721)
o Initiation of QT-prolonging medication and dose changes q8-12h
o Overdose of proarrhythmic drug
o New bradyarrhythmia
o Severe hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia Illustration: Modified from Circ EP 2019;12:12

panels.title: MANAGEMENT OF ACQUIRED LONG QT
panels.text:
MANAGEMENT OF ACQUIRED LONG QT
• Stop offending drug if QTc >500ms or increase in QTc of >60ms
• ECG should be checked for bradyarrhythmias & signs of impending TdP (R on T, above). Stop drugs causing bradycardia.
• Check electrolytes & replenish to supratherapeutic levels (K: 4.5-5, Mg: 2-2.5)
• If patient develops TdP: See ACLS: Wide complex tachycardia page
Amanda Jowell

topics.text:
Cardiology QTc Prolongation
DEFINITION (Circ 2009; 119: e241)
• QT interval correlates with repolarization time of ventricles
• Normal: ≤460ms; Borderline (adult): 460-479ms (female), 450-459ms (male)
• Measure from beginning of QRS to end of T wave in a lead with T wave > 2mm
(best in II, V5), define end point using tangent from peak of steepest slope to
isoelectric line; can use ECG or caliper function on telemetry
• QTc is QT corrected for HR; linear (i.e., Hodges/Framingham) formulas are
recommended by AHA (J Electrocardiology 2004;37:81)
• Can be calculated using MDCalc: Framingham and Fridericia provide best rate
correction and mortality prediction (JAHA 2016;5:e003264)
ASSESSMENT OF QTC WITH UNDERLYING WIDE QRS (Heart Rhythm 2014;11:2273)
• Wide QRS (BBB/V-paced) lengthens QT interval; calculate using Mayo calculator, or with rough estimate using QT - (0.5*QRS).
Must still account for HR (Heart Rhythm. 2014 Dec;11(12)).
CONGENITAL LONG-QT SYNDROMES
• Majority of pts are asymptomatic, often discovered on ECG or QTc prolonged more than should be expected by drugs
• Sx: presyncope/syncope, hemodynamic compromise, sudden cardiac death; triggered by exercise, stress
• Tx: beta blocker for all, ICD if previous cardiac arrest and expected survival >1y (Class 1A Recommendation) (Circ 2006;114:e385)
o BB thought to reduce early after-depolarizations and transmural dispersion of repolarizations, which can trigger arrhythmias
DRUG-INDUCED PROLONGED QT INTERVAL (Heart 2003;89:1363; NEJM 2004;350:1013)
• Drugs inhibit rapid K+ current causing prolonged ventricular repolarization & exaggerate heterogeneity in repolarization times in
different layers of myocardium leading to reentry and tachyarrhythmia
Danger of prolonged QT = increased risk of Torsades de Pointes (TdP), which can degenerate into VF
Longer QT increases risk for “R on T” phenomenon and development of TdP (higher risk if PVCs)

panels.title: DEFINITIONS AND EVALUATION
panels.text:
DEFINITIONS AND EVALUATION
Myocardial injury: defined as any patient with troponin >99th percentile without evidence of myocardial ischemia (sx of ischemia, new
ischemic ECG changes, new wall-motion abnormalities, and/or acute coronary thrombus on angio). May be acute or chronic.
Myocardial infarction: myocardial necrosis (trop >99th percentile + ) w/ ischemia (4th universal def. of MI, types 1-5: JACC 2018;72:2231)
• Type 1 MI: spontaneous coronary plaque rupture, erosion  intraluminal thrombus
• Type 2 MI: flow/O2 supply-demand mismatch that is not atherothrombosis – most commonly due to sepsis/infection, arrhythmias,
severe anemia, renal failure, surgery, hypertension, and heart failure; other causes include vasospasm, microvascular ischemia (e.g.
Takotsubo), thromboembolism (Circulation 2019;140:1661).
o Must have a clear precipitating factor. If not, treat as a type 1 MI until further evaluation
o 50-70% have obstructive CAD – reasonable to initiate ASA, BB, and high-intensity statin

panels.title: R EVASCULARIZATION
panels.text:
R EVASCULARIZATION
STEMI
o Primary PCI (PPCI) recommended revasc strategy for pts w/STEMI <48h symptom onset (PCI center: aim<60 min to wire crossing)
o PPCI regardless of symptom onset if cardiogenic shock, malignant arrhythmia (recurrent sustained VT/VF), persistent STE and/or CP
o PPCI>48h symptom onset not indicated in stable pts (NEJM 2006;355:2395)
o If PPCI not possible within 120 min first med contact (and <24h symptom onset), fibrinolysis: Aim<10 min to lytic bolus (Tenecteplase
preferred) w/ immediate transfer to PCI center. Discuss antithrombotic therapy w/cardiology. Contraindicated in ↑bleeding risk (esp
ICH), suspected dissection, ischemic stroke <3 months prior, severe HTN
NSTE-ACS (NSTEMI/UA)
o Multiple risk models incl GRACE, TIMI. GRACE score is based on predictors of 6mo mortality (BMJ 2006;333:1091)
o Four subgroups for urgency to revascularization (JACC 2014;64:e139)
1. Very high risk (“immediate invasive,” within 2h): refractory/recurrent angina, hemodynamic or electrical instability,
mechanical complications, recurrent dynamic ECG changes suggestive of ischemia
2. High risk (“early invasive,” within 24h): temporal change in troponin, ECG changes (transient STE, STD, TWI), high risk pt
(GRACE>140)
a. Conflicting results between TIMAC (NEJM 2009;360:2165) and VERDICT (Circ 2018;138:2741) trials about outcome benefit of
early cath. However, both show improved outcomes with early cath in patients with GRACE >140
3. Intermediate risk (“delayed invasive,” within 72h): none of above but risk factors at baseline (e.g. EF <40%, GFR <60)
4. Low risk (“ischemia guided,” no cath): no risk factors, GRACE <109, TIMI 0-1 OR not good candidate for angiography

panels.text:
PCI vs CABG: Selection of revascularization strategy should be based on the acuity of the patient’s condition, the angiographic
characteristics of the culprit lesion, and the complexity of the patient’s anatomy and, when appropriate, should include a Heart Team
discussion (Guideline: Circulation 2022;145:4). CABG often preferred for 3VD (NEJM 2009;360:961), L main disease (NEJM 2016;375:2223),
2VD with prox LAD stenosis or EF <50%, DM + 2VD w/ involvement of LAD (NEJM 2012;367:2375).
Multivessel Disease PCI Strategies
o STEMI w/o cardiogenic shock: complete revascularization strategy (culprit + non-culprit) has risk of CV death and MI at 3y
(COMPLETE, NEJM 2019;381:1411)
o STEMI OR NSTE-ACS + cardiogenic shock: culprit-lesion only PCI has a risk of death/RRT (CULPRIT-SHOCK, NEJM
2018;379:1699). Consider staged complete revascularization
o NSTE-ACS w/o cardiogenic shock: complete revascularization strategy (BIOVASC, Lancet 2023;401:1172)

panels.title: ADJUNCTS TO REVASCULARIZATION
panels.text:
ADJUNCTS TO REVASCULARIZATION
Adjuncts at Presentation:
1. ASA: established mortality benefit, give to all pts in an immediate load/maintenance strategy (325mg/81mg) (Lancet 1988;2:8607)
2. Peri-Intervention Anticoagulation: start on Dx of ACS. Usually stopped after PCI if no additional indication for AC (eg Afib, PE). If
no PCI and medically managed, usually d/c at 48h if ECG changes improving and c/f ongoing ischemia resolved (BMJ 1996;313:652). If
chronically on warfarin/DOAC, discuss transition to short acting AC with pharmacy pre-cath.
o UFH: Standard. Start gtt w/ bolus and use low intensity PTT goal (50-70). Anti-Xa protocol also available. No bolus if giving
lytics or if on warfarin and INR<2
o LMWH: possible reduction in death w/ minimal evidence for major bleeding, trials vs UFH largely null (BMJ 2012;344:e553)
o Fondaparinux: preferred to UFH/LMWH if medically managed. Contraindicated in PCI catheter thrombosis/complications
(JAMA 2006;295:1519)
o GPIIb/IIa Inhibitors: eptifibatide (Integrilin) . Initiated in cath lab if PCI high-risk (extensive thrombus)
o Bivalirudin/Argatroban: direct thrombin inhibitor, preferred for patients w/ HIT. Emerging evidence suggests benefit over UFH
in STEMI (BRIGHT-4 Lancet 2022;400:1847)
3. Statin: atorvastatin 80mg daily regardless of baseline LDL (NEJM 2004;350:1495)
o Early high-dose statin within 24-96h may reduce death/adverse cardiac events if given pre-PCI (JACC 2009;54:2157; JAMA
2018;319:1331). Early anti-inflammatory effect may stabilize plaque (JAMA 2001;285:1711; JAMA 2004;291:1071)
o If very high risk clinical ASCVD w/ LDL-c >70 mg/dL, add ezetimibe and consider PCSK9i (JACC 2019;73:3168)
4. Nitrates: TNG SL (0.3-0.6mg) x3, if refractory → gtt (start 5-10mcg/min titrate to chest pain free). Nitropaste and gtt have shorter
half-life than SL if c/f HoTN. No mortality benefit. Caution in inferior MI/RVMI, SBP<100, or PDEi use in last 48h. If refractory CP
indication for earlier cath.
5. Morphine: not recommended. Consider only if unacceptable level of pain refractory to TNG, careful if suspicious for inferior MI/RVMI
6. Discontinue NSAIDs: risk of mortality, re-infarction, HF, and myocardial rupture after ACS
Adjuncts to start within 24h or Post-Revasc
7. P2Y12 Inhibitors: . Controversial benefit & may delay CABG by 5-
7d (Circulation 2022;145:4). )
o Ticagrelor: mortality compared to clopidogrel w/o increasing major bleeding. Reversible with platelet transfusion. Side effect:
dyspnea (14-21%, often mild & transient, but can be severe enough to warrant discontinuation), risk of pneumonitis w/ alveolar
hemorrhage. Avoid in liver disease, prior CVA, oral AC (PLATO, NEJM 2009;361:1045).
o Prasugrel: death, MI, CVA compared to ticag (NEJM 2019;381:1524). Contraindicated if prior TIA/CVA, wt <60kg, or >75y
o Clopidogrel: death, repeat MI when load/maintenance with PCI (Lancet 2001;358:527I). Prodrug, metabolized by CYP219, less
effective in those with LOF allele (NEJM 2009;360:354). May benefit from PPI ppx for ↓UGIB (NEJM 2010;363:1909). ↓Bleeding
compared to ticagrelor and prasugrel but ↑ischemic events (Circulation 2020;142:150).
o Cangrelor: IV reversible inhibitor with immediate onset and return of platelet function in 1h.
DAPT duration: Default 12 months after ACS. Use DAPT score to help risk stratify. Evolving movement to shorten DAPT duration
(Select DAPT trials: TWILIGHT, TICO, STOPDAPT-2, SMART CHOICE, GLOBAL LEADERS, MASTER DAPT, HOST-EXAM)
Bottom line: In select patients, single agent P2Y12 inhibitor after 1-3 months (vs. longer duration DAPT) is non-inferior in
reduction of cardiovascular events, with reduced bleeding. Decisions on DAPT should involve interventional cardiology
o If on longterm AC (eg AFib, PE): P2Y12 inhibitor + DOAC > triple therapy. bleeding and non-inferior for ischemic events
(AUGUSTUS NEJM 2019;380;1509; RE-DUAL PCI NEJM 2017;377:1513; NEJM 2016; 375:2423). (Guideline JACC 2021;77:629).
▪ Common example: initiate triple therapy (ASA/clopidogrel/AC) for 1-4wks and then d/c ASA → AC + clopidogrel
8. Beta Blockers: start within 24h (1B for STEMI, 1A for NSTE-ACS), mortality benefit. Consider early initiation if ischemic arrhythmias
present. Not indicated for stable ischemic heart disease s/p cath, but rec’d after CABG (Circulation 2022;145:4). Long term BB s/p MI
w/ LVEF >50%, does not reduce mortality or recurrent MI (NEJM 2024;390:1372)
o Caution in decompensated HF, risk for cardiogenic shock (>70y, SBP <120, HR >110 or <60)
o Contraindications: shock, cocaine-induced MI, PR>240ms, 2nd or 3rd degree AVB, severe bronchospasm (Lancet 2005;366:1622)
9. ACEi or ARB: start ACE within 24h in all patients if BP/renal function normal; mortality benefit in anterior STEMI; use ARB if intolerant
of ACE. ARB > ACE in patients with HF or LVEF <40% (Circulation 2008; 117:269).
10. Aldosterone antagonist: s/p MI on ACE and BB, and have LVEF<=40 + DM or sx of HF (Circulation 2008; 117:269)
11. Lifestyle: smoking cessation, BP <130/80 (esp. if comorbid DM or CKD), cardiac rehab, depression screening; Flu vaccination

DEFINITIONS AND EVALUATION
Myocardial injury: defined as any patient with troponin >99th percentile without evidence of myocardial ischemia (sx of ischemia, new
ischemic ECG changes, new wall-motion abnormalities, and/or acute coronary thrombus on angio). May be acute or chronic.
Myocardial infarction: myocardial necrosis (trop >99th percentile + ) w/ ischemia (4th universal def. of MI, types 1-5: JACC 2018;72:2231)
• Type 1 MI: spontaneous coronary plaque rupture, erosion  intraluminal thrombus
• Type 2 MI: flow/O2 supply-demand mismatch that is not atherothrombosis – most commonly due to sepsis/infection, arrhythmias,
severe anemia, renal failure, surgery, hypertension, and heart failure; other causes include vasospasm, microvascular ischemia (e.g.
Takotsubo), thromboembolism (Circulation 2019;140:1661).
o Must have a clear precipitating factor. If not, treat as a type 1 MI until further evaluation

8. Beta Blockers: start within 24h (1B for STEMI, 1A for NSTE-ACS), mortality benefit. Consider early initiation if ischemic arrhythmias
present. Not indicated for stable ischemic heart disease s/p cath, but rec’d after CABG (Circulation 2022;145:4). Long term BB s/p MI
w/ LVEF >50%, does not reduce mortality or recurrent MI (NEJM 2024;390:1372)
o Caution in decompensated HF, risk for cardiogenic shock (>70y, SBP <120, HR >110 or <60)
o Contraindications: shock, cocaine-induced MI, PR>240ms, 2nd or 3rd degree AVB, severe bronchospasm (Lancet 2005;366:1622)
9. ACEi or ARB: start ACE within 24h in all patients if BP/renal function normal; mortality benefit in anterior STEMI; use ARB if intolerant
of ACE. ARB > ACE in patients with HF or LVEF <40% (Circulation 2008; 117:269).
10. Aldosterone antagonist: s/p MI on ACE and BB, and have LVEF<=40 + DM or sx of HF (Circulation 2008; 117:269)
11. Lifestyle: smoking cessation, BP <130/80 (esp. if comorbid DM or CKD), cardiac rehab, depression screening; Flu vaccination

URGENT ASSESSMENT OF POST-MI COMPLICATION
• PAGE Cardiology (STAT)
• Assess for instability, focused physical exam (new murmur, pericardial friction rub, elevated JVP, crackles, access site(s))

topics.title: Cardiac Catheterization

panels.title: Source content
panels.text: • Note: RAO caudal: best overall view & best for LCx; LAO caudal: LM, prox LAD, prox LCx; LAO + RAO cran: mid+distal LAD

panels.title: LEFT VS RIGHT HEART CATHETERIZATION
panels.text:
LEFT VS RIGHT HEART CATHETERIZATION
• LHC: Arterial access (radial, fem). Assess coronary anatomy/lesions (described as coronary angiogram), LV & Ao pressures; PCI
• RHC: Venous access (IJ, fem). Assess hemodynamics (see Pulmonary Artery Catherization); cardiac biopsies (usually RV)

panels.title: CORONARY ANATOMY
panels.text:
CORONARY ANATOMY
• LCA and RCA & their branches create two rings around the heart: RCA + LCX in AV groove; LAD + PDA in IV groove
• 80% of PDA arises from RCA (right dominant), thus inferior MI more likely due to RCA lesion; 10% from LCx; 10% co-dominant

panels.title: PREPARATION FOR CATHETERIZATION
panels.text:
PREPARATION FOR CATHETERIZATION
• NPO MN vs clear liquid diet at midnight, then NPO 2hr prior (EHJ 2024:45:47) ; INR<2 for radial, <1.8 for fem/IJ; monitor Cr, no ppx
abx. Cont ASA, statin, BB. Hold AC (ellucid): UFH gtt (hold when on call), LMWH (hold tx dose 24h prior, DVT ppx 12h prior), DOACs
>48hr or >72hr if CrCl<30. Hold metformin (1d pre, 2d post), may hold ACEi or SGLT2i (procedure dependent)
• Document b/l radial, femoral, popliteal, DP pulses, & Allen’s test. Check for bruits. Note history of HIT, PAD, Ao aneurysm/dissection
• Contrast allergy: pre-tx w/ steroids & benadryl if patient has documented allergy.
• Respiratory distress: patient will need to lie flat; consider intubation if prohibitive hypoxemia/pulmonary edema
• Pre-hydration w/ crystalloids and NAC/bicarb have not been shown to prevent CIN in most patients with moderate CKD (Lancet
2017;389:1312; NEJM 2018;378:603); CIN risk calculator

panels.title: PERCUTANEOUS CORONARY INTERVENTION CONSIDERATIONS
panels.text:
PERCUTANEOUS CORONARY INTERVENTION CONSIDERATIONS
• Access: fewer bleeding/vascular complications if radial (vs femoral) esp for PCI iso ACS, possible death in ACS (JACC 2018;71:1167);
due to radial vasospasm, CCB and/or nitrogylcerin is administered along with UFH to prevent arterial occlusion
• Identifying HD significant lesions: fractional flow reserve (FFR), diastolic hyperemia-free ratio (DFR), and instant wave free ratio (iFR)
assess functional impact of lesion; intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) evaluates lumen diameter, lesion length, and lesion calcification
• Contraindications to stents: predicted DAPT non-adherence, anticipated major surgery within treatment time, elevated bleeding risk
• Antiplatelet: 81mg ASA indefinitely (Circ 2016;134:e123). P2Y12 inhibitor post cath. DAPT duration decided with interventional team
o Not high bleeding risk: ACS → 12mo DAPT; stable IHD → ≥6mo DAPT if DES or ≥1mo if BMS
o High bleeding risk: ACS → 6mo DAPT, consider DAPT 1-3mo followed by P2Y12i; stable IHD → ≥3mo DAPT if DES or ≥1mo if
BMS, consider 1-3mo DAPT followed by P2Y12i (JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2024;17:2197)

panels.title: POST-PROCEDURE CARE
panels.text:
POST-PROCEDURE CARE
• Femoral access: 4-6h bedrest (HOB<30°) after procedure. Closure devices decrease time needed for bedrest
o Groin checks immediately, 6h, 8h post-procedure: check b/l pulses, palpate for pulsatile masses, auscultate for bruits
o Sheaths: usually removed when PTT<60, confirm with interventional fellow; only fellows remove sheaths
• Radial access: TR band for 4-6h driven by RN protocol. If paresthesias/numbness, examine, check finger sat probe for perfusion, can
remove several mLs of air from band if necessary and if no complications. NOTE: if hematoma do not remove until fellow assesses

panels.title: POST-CATHERIZATION COMPLICATIONS
panels.text:
POST-CATHERIZATION COMPLICATIONS
• Access site complications: always inform the interventional fellow who performed the procedure, diagnose by exam and US
o Hematoma: mass w/o bruit. Apply compression. Fellow may recommend FemoStop device if unable to control
o Pseudoaneurysm: pulsatile mass with bruit at access site. Tx w/ compression; if <2cm, may require thrombin injection or
surgery if >2 cm. Urgent arterial US & Vascular Surgery consult
o AV fistula: continuous bruit with no mass. Evaluate w/ arterial US. Surgical repair usually necessary
o Limb ischemia: from thrombus, dissection, or malpositioned closure device. Evaluate pulses, limb warmth, & PVR
o Retroperitoneal bleed: presents within hours post-cath, often with hemodynamic instability ± flank pain ± ecchymoses. STAT
CT A/P if stable. Obtain large bore IV access, IVF, transfuse, discuss with attending about stopping/reversing anticoagulation
• Other complications:
o Infection: higher risk with vascular closure devices
o Atheroembolism: eosinophilia; livedo reticularis; blue toes; mesenteric ischemia; acute, subacute, or chronic renal dysfunction
o CIN: occurs within 24-72h with peak Cr 1-5d post contrast load; risk correlated with contrast load and initial GFR
o Tamponade: narrow PP, hypotension 2/2 coronary/cardiac perf. Check pulsus (>10 mmHg), STAT TTE, alert cath fellow.
o MI/CVA: due to in-stent thrombosis (MI) or distal embolization post-cath (CVA). Discuss all CP/neuro changes with cath fellow
o Radiation injury: more common in CTO cases; occurs days to weeks after PCI; ranges from erythema to skin ulceration
o Delayed Hemostasis: apply indirect pressure several cm cranial to site of skin access. Page gen cards fellow to discuss
escalation to cath fellow/vasc surg (see ellucid escalation pathway)

CORONARY ANATOMY

topics.title: Non-Invasive Cardiac Testing

panels.title: BASICS
panels.text:
BASICS
• Non-invasive cardiac testing includes functional and anatomic testing
• Approach to testing: 1) clinical question being asked, 2) symptom acuity, 3) baseline CVD risk/known CAD hx, 4) patient-specific C.I.
• For guideline-based assistance in decision making, use Stressing Wisely. For examples of (+) and (-) tests, use Radiopaedia.

panels.title: ROLE OF NON-INVASIVE CARDIAC TESTING IN CHEST PAIN EVALUATION
panels.text:
ROLE OF NON-INVASIVE CARDIAC TESTING IN CHEST PAIN EVALUATION
Source: 2021 ACC/AHA Guidelines for Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain (Circ 2021;144:e368-e454)
Deciding between CCTA (anatomic) and stress imaging in an intermediate-high risk patient:
• CCTA favored: Age<65y and no prior CAD, rule out obstructive CAD, detect non-obstructive CAD, prior functional study w/o
conclusive results, bypass graft assessment, known anomalous coronaries, parallel evaluation of aorta, pulmonary arteries, or LAA
• Stress imaging favored: Age>65y, if known >50% (obstructive) CAD to assess for specific areas of ischemia, prior CCTA w/o
conclusive results, parallel evaluation for scar or microvascular dysfunction (PET or CMR)
• CCTA has higher sensitivity and similar angiography rates as conventional stress imaging; however, CCTA may lead to better
outcomes overall as it can detect non-obstructive CAD and therefore drive preventive care (NEJM 2018;379:924)

panels.title: STRESS/FUNCTIONAL TESTING
panels.text:
STRESS/FUNCTIONAL TESTING
• Indications:
o Diagnose CAD: Workup stable angina in pts with intermediate-high risk of CAD. Consider spectrum of non-invasive tests vs. cath
in intermediate-risk pts presenting with more acute sx. Not indicated in pts with no symptoms or at low risk
o Evaluate new or changing sx concerning for ischemia in pts with known CAD
o Post-revascularization: Evaluate pts with angina or asymptomatic pts if incomplete revasc or >2y post-PCI/5y post-CABG.
o Pre-op risk assessment: If indicated (see Perioperative Medicine)
o Other: Newly diagnosed HF or cardiomyopathy likely secondary to ischemia, functional capacity (for exercise prescription),
viability testing, valvular disorders, dobutamine stress echo in LFLG AS, quantify microvascular disease (PET)
• Contraindications: Untreated ACS, MI within 2d, high risk or LM CAD, uncontrolled arrhythmia, ADHF, severe AS or HOCM, recent
DVT/PE, acute myo-/peri-/endocarditis, aortic dissection, uncontrolled HTN
• Preparation: NPO 3h prior, longer if imaging or adenosine. Must reverse DNR/DNI for test
o If the question is “Does the patient have CAD?”  hold BB and nitrates
o If the question is “How well are meds working in known CAD?”  continue BB and nitrates
o Hold BB >24h for dobutamine stress test; hold caffeine >12h for adenosine
▪ Positive test results: Optimize medical rx. Decision re: angiography/revascularization varies by pt (degree of sx,
tolerance of medical therapy). In ISCHEMIA trial, initial revasc vs. medical therapy did not reduce risk of ischemic
CV events for pts with moderate to severe stable ischemic heart disease (NEJM 2020;382:1395). In pts w/ stable
angina, PCI does not increase exercise tolerance (Lancet 2018;391:31), but for pts who cannot tolerate medical
therapy, PCI improved symptoms (NEJM 2023;389:2319)
• Caveats:
o Majority of vulnerable plaques are angiographically insignificant (<70% stenosis)  CCTA more sensitive for their detection
o Angiographically significant 3VD may produce false-negative vasodilator stress test  ”balanced ischemia”
▪ Balanced ischemia can be detected as transient ischemic dilatation (enlargement of LV cavity during stress)
▪ PET has higher accuracy in 3VD than SPECT/MIBI, because PET quantifies blood flow
• ,
.
•
Spencer Flynn

panels.title: Source content
panels.text:
Approach to choosing a stressor and evaluation modality:
• See Table 5 for full list of contraindications by test type (Circ 2021;144:e368-e454).
Choosing a stressor:
o Exercise: Preferred if patient can reach goal exertion. More relevant to real-world stress
o Adenosine/Regadenoson:
▪ Mechanism: Vasodilation via cAMP, detect ischemia by coronary steal (stenosed coronary arteries are unable to further
dilate, creating a relative perfusion deficit in diseased vessels).
▪ Side effects: Wheezing, bradycardia, HoTN. Caution if ACTIVE bronchospasm, high grade AVB, SSS, severe AS
o Regadenoson (vs adenosine) has decreased respiratory/conduction side effects, is more cost-effective in obese pts,
but caution if seizure hx (reversal agent aminophylline seizure risk)
o Dobutamine:
▪ Mechanism: Positive inotropy and chronotropy via β-1 receptor agonism. Extremely high dose (up to 40 mcg/kg/min)
▪ Side effects: tachyarrhyth. Caution if MI <48h, hx malignant arrhyth, sev AS, HOCM, sev HTN, sev PAH, aortic dissection
Choosing an evaluation modality:
o ECG: Only used as stand-alone with exercise. Do not use with any longstanding ST/T wave abnormalities.
o TTE: Can define ischemia severity and risk-stratify. Additional info on hemodynamics/valves. ECG also obtained simultaneously.
▪ Do not use in pts with LBBB, V-pacing, or extensive wall motion abnormalities at rest
o Nuclear imaging (PET or SPECT/MIBI myocardial perfusion imaging):
▪ Uses a radiotracer (MIBI in SPECT, multiple options in PET) to detect areas of perfusion between rest and stress states.
Can measure LV function, transient LV dilatation, myocardial blood flow reserve. PET can detect microvascular ischemia.
▪ More expensive than TTE & high amount of radiation (SPECT > PET)
▪ PET more Sn & Sp than SPECT with faster image acquisition. Less widely available & more expensive. Additional uses for
imaging in rheumatologic (i.e. cardiac sarcoid) and oncologic contexts (i.e. cardiac myxoma, metastases).
o Cardiac MRI (CMR):
▪ Localize ischemia and infarction, assess LV and RV function, determine myocardial viability. Can also detect microvascular
dysfunction and tissue properties of the heart (inflammation, scarring, infiltration, cardiac tumors, pericardial disease)
Exercise Tolerance Test (ETT):
• Approach: ETT refers to exercise + ECG (cheap, available), or exercise + imaging eval (TTE, SPECT) (sensitivity)
• Protocols: Bruce (large changes in workload between stages), modified Bruce (for less fit pts  adds stages of lower workload)
• Assess: exercise duration, METs, BP/HR response, HR recovery, double product (HR x SBP), Duke Treadmill Score (estimates risk of
CAD in pts w/ chest pain undergoing exercise stress testing (Circ 1998;98:1622)).
• Diagnostic if: >85% max-predict HR (220-age), peak double product (HRxBP) >20k, HR recovery (HR – HR ) >12,
peak 1min post-exercise
STEs - also localize to vascular territory
• Increased probability of ischemia with:  # of leads with STD especially horizontal or downsloping,  degree of max STD,  METs
when ECG changes occur, ventricular ectopy during recovery, increased time to recovery of ECG, failure of SBP to rise with exercise.
Viability testing:
• Indication: Determine viability of ischemic myocardium (assess for hibernating tissue) that may be salvaged w/ revascularization.
• Modalities: SPECT, PET, TTE, MRI with exercise or pharmacologic stress. Looking for metabolic or contractile reserve.

panels.title: ANATOMIC TESTING
panels.text:
ANATOMIC TESTING
Coronary CTA (CCTA):
• Indications:
o Evaluate for the presence and extent of CAD. Primarily anatomic info, though offers plaque characterization and CT FFR.
o Asymptomatic pts: NOT for screening use. Low-risk pts with sx: high NPV (99%) for CAD rule-out (JACC 2008;52:1724). Moderate-
risk pts with sx: reasonable for risk stratification (especially after equivocal stress test).
• Preparation: Requires cardiac gating (goal HR 60-70, may need to give BB) and respiratory gating (breath hold for 5+ sec).
• Results:
o 2y ACS risk significantly elevated if high-risk plaque (16%) and/or stenotic disease (6%) (JACC 2015;28:337)
o Higher Sn & Sp for coronary stenosis compared to cMRI (Annals 2010;152:167)
• Caveats: Less useful in pts with extensive calcifications (older) or stented vessels due to “blooming” artifact (cannot eval patency).
Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) Scan:
• Indications:
o Risk-assessment for ASCVD risk stratification. Used to guide decision-making for primary prevention/statin therapy in
asymptomatic pts, ≥40y at intermediate-risk (7.5-19.9% 10y ASCVD risk). DO NOT use in symptomatic pts or high risk pts.
• Preparation: Non-gated, non-contrast (if done independent of CCTA) CT scan.
• Results: MESA score accounts for CAC score and is able to refine 10 year risk estimates
o If CAC score 0 and pt without significant risk factors, reasonable to defer statin therapy for up to 5 years (Circ 2019;140:496).
o If CAC score ≥100 or >75%ile for age & gender, recommend aggressive lifestyle changes, ASCVD RF modification (BP,
smoking cessation, diabetes treatment), & statin therapy (JACC 2019;73:285)
Cardiac MRI: provides both stress/functional and anatomic testing options
Spencer Flynn
20

CLINICAL QUESTIONS AND ASSOCIATED TTE FINDINGS
• Right heart strain in acute PE: RV WMA or hypokinesis, RV dilation (RV:LV ratio >1), interventricular septal bowing, IVC collapse, “D-sign”: septal
flattening, “McConnell’s sign”: RV free wall akinesia w/ normal RV apex motion (77% Sn, 94% Sp for acute PE)
• Tamponade: effusion, RA collapse in systole (earliest sonographic sign; high sensitivity), RV collapse in diastole (high specificity), respirophasic
variation in mitral inflow velocity by > 25%), interventricular septal bowing, plethoric IVC (no  w/ inspiration)

• Diastolic dysfunction: LA enlargement, E/e’ >14, LVH ( )
• Constrictive pericarditis: thickened or hyperechoic pericardium, abnormal septal motion, respiratory variation in ventricular size, dilated IVC
• Cardiac amyloid: biatrial enlargement, increased LV and RV wall thickening, valvular thickening, diastolic dysfunction, paradoxical LFLG AS, strain
imaging with reduced global longitudinal strain and apical sparing

topics.title: Heart Failure

panels.title: BASIC FRAMEWORK
panels.text:
BASIC FRAMEWORK
Diagnosis of heart failure vs cardiomyopathy (CM)
• Heart failure is a clinical diagnosis – requires signs/symptoms of volume
overload (e.g. orthopnea, leg swelling, crackles, ↑JVP) attributable to a
structural or functional impairment in ventricular ejection or filling
• Heart failure ≠ cardiomyopathy – a CM is an abnormality in myocardial
structure or function, usually visualized by TTE (does not require
signs/symptoms of volume overload)
Classifications of heart failure
• LVEF classes: HFpEF (LVEF >50%), HFmrEF (‘mildly reduced’ EF;
LVEF 41-49%), HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), HFimpEF (‘improved’ EF; previous
LVEF ≤40% and a follow-up measurement of LFEF > 40%)
• ACC/AHA Stage and NYHA Functional Class (see Figure)
Identifying underlying etiology
Category Cardiomyopathy etiologies
Most common ischemic, hypertensive, valvular
Metabolic diabetic, nutritional deficiency (e.g. beriberi)
High-output septic, peripartum, hyperthyroid, anemia, liver failure, Paget’s, AV shunts
Toxins/drugs alcohol, cocaine/amphetamines, chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors
Infectious HIV, coxsackie, echovirus, EBV, CMV, Lyme, Chagas disease, tuberculosis
Infiltrative amyloidosis (ATTR or AL), hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, Löffler’s
Genetic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/HOCM, ARVC, familial neuromuscular disorders, glycogen storage disorders, LVNC
Inflammatory connective tissue diseases, giant cell myocarditis
Other pulmonary (cor pulmonale), stress-induced (Takotsubo), tachyarrhythmia-induced, pericardial disease (e.g.
constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion), radiation, carcinoid, idiopathic
NOTE: CM can be additional defined as ‘dilated,’ ‘hypertrophic,’ and ‘restrictive’ based on morphology/structure seen on imaging
Workup
• Initial workup: signs/sxs of volume overload, troponin, NTproBNP, ECG, tele, CXR, TTE
• Ischemic CM workup: family hx, smoking hx, lipid panel, A1c, see Non-Invasive Testing and Cardiac Catherization
• Non-ischemic CM workup: family hx, med hx, substance use hx, tox screen, β-hCG, iron studies, SPEP/UPEP/FLC, TSH, HIV, ANA
• Extended workup (when applicable): chest CT, cardiac MRI, RHC, endomyocardial biopsy, PYP scan, viral serology panel, Lyme
serologies, T. cruzi serologies, ACE level, thiamine/carnitine/selenium, genetic testing, antimyosin Ab
Management of heart failure
• Treat the underlying causes of (1) cardiomyopathy and (2) decompensation triggers
• Basic elements of treatment: diuresis, afterload reduction, consideration of device/advanced therapies
• Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT):
o HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFimpEF = BB, ACEi/ARB/ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i 2022 ACC/AHA HF Guidelines:
o HFpEF = MRA, SGLT2i Circ 2022;145:895
• Cardiomyopathy-specific interventions: ischemic = PCI, CABG; valvular = TAVR, MitraClip,
other valve interventions; tachyarrhytmia-induced = ablation, PPM, CRT; ATTR amyloid = tafamadis TTR deposition (NEJM
2018;379:1007), acoramadis, vutrisiran; sarcoid = prednisone, steroid-sparing IST

panels.title: CONSIDERATIONS FOR SELECT CARDIOMYOPATHIES
panels.text:
CONSIDERATIONS FOR SELECT CARDIOMYOPATHIES
Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) (Circulation 2024;149 :e1239)
Characteristics: LV and/or RV hypertrophy ± LVOT dynamic obstruction (HOCM), diastolic dysfxn, ischemia, MR; risk of SCD
Exam: SEM at LLSB/apex that augments with Valsalva or on standing (due to preload); S2 paradox split, S4
Dx: ECG (prominent voltages w/ depol abnormalities, large Q waves in inferior/lateral leads, LAD, negative T waves in V2-V4 (apical
HCM), TTE (LVH >15mm, SAM of MV, outflow tract gradient +/- provocative test), cMRI (late gadolinium enhancement [LGE] = fibrosis)
Clinical genetic testing (mutation in ~70%) helpful for family screening; not useful for dx or risk stratification
Tx: avoid volume depletion or high dose vasodilators (may worsen obstruction); phenylephrine is pressor of choice if no response to
IVF bolus for HoTN (afterload, stents open LVOT). Activity restriction, meds (disopyramide, BB > verapamil). Cardiac myosin inhibitors
(e.g. aficamten, mavacamten) if LVEF ≥ 55% (VALOR-HCM); septal ablation or surgical myectomy if medically refractory, ICD ifhigh risk
Risk factors for SCD/VT: prior VT/SCD/unexplained syncope; FHx of SCD in 1° relative; massive LVH (>30mm); NSVT on Holter;
abnormal BP response to exercise; burden of LGE on cMRI; h/o suspected cardiac syncope; EF<50%
• Amyloidosis (AL, TTR): HF + amyloid findings (e.g. renal), low voltage ECG, thick LV/RV on TTE, LGE in subendocardium on cMRI
• Hemochromatosis: hereditary or secondary, ECG with SVT, dilated LV on TTE, iron overload on T2 protocol of cMRI
• Sarcoidosis: ECG with atypical infarct pattern or block, patchy enhancement of basal and LV walls on cMRI

panels.title: ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE MANAGEMENT – FLOOR/SDU
panels.text:
ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE MANAGEMENT – FLOOR/SDU
Frederick Lang, Emily Manning
22

panels.title: Source content
panels.text:
Identify hemodynamic profile and triage accordingly (JACC 2019;74:1966)
• Warm vs Cold: consider AMS, lactate, cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure
• Dry vs Wet: presence vs absence of congestion
• Evaluate for pulmonary congestion on exam. Pulm edema may be
absent on CXR due to lymphatic compensation (Chest 2004;125:669)
• Majority of HFrEF and HFpEF pts will be warm and wet
• See ‘Right Ventricular Failure’ for special considerations for patients
with primarily right-sided heart disease
History
• Identify decompensation triggers: Mnemonic FAILURE – F = forgot meds, A = arrhythmia/anemia/afterload, I = infection/ischemia, L =
lifestyle (salty diet), U = upregulation of cardiac output (e.g. pregnancy, hyperthyroid), R = renal failure, E = embolism. Other triggers:
progression of CM, inadequate diuretic dose, meds (NSAIDs, steroids, CCB, anthracyclines), toxins (EtOH), new/worsened valve
• HF history (prior CM dx, dry weight, last NTproBNP, last TTE/EF, prior ischemic w/u, outpt cardiologist), accurate PAML, social/fam hx
Admission considerations
• Admission orders: tele, 2g Na-restricted diet, daily standing weights, strict I/Os, DVT ppx, (SDU only) electrolyte replenishment scales
• SDU admission indications: EF <25%, NTproBNP ≥ 2,500, arrhythmia-induced HF. Black & Latinx pts w/ HF are less likely to be
admitted to cardiology services, contributing to racial inequities in HF outcomes (Circ Heart Fail 2019;12:e006214)
• Avoid: CCB (esp. non-dihydropyridines), NSAIDs, flecainide
• Check NT-proBNP (& weight) on admission. ADHF unlikely if NT-proBNP <300 (NPV 98%), likely if >450 (>900 if age >50) (Am J
Cardiol 2005;95;948). Difficult to interpret in CKD/dialysis. May be falsely low in obesity, HFpEF
• Screen for and treat iron deficiency in all HF pts independent of Hgb (JACC HF 2019;7:36)
o Dx: ferritin <100 or ferritin <300 + TSat <20% (JACC 2017;70:776)
o Tx: replete with IV iron (JACC 2018;71:782) to sx, functional capacity, and possibly improve outcomes (NEJM 2023;389:975)
Early/acute management
• Diuresis: CVP, PCWP to optimize Starling curve mechanics & relieve sx (NEJM 2017;377:1964; JACC 2020;75:1178)
o Initial tx: IV loop (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide), start w/ 20-40mg IV furosemide if diuretic-naïve otherwise start w/ 2-2.5x
home dose (IV/PO). No difference b/w continuous gtt vs bolus (NEJM 2011;364:797). See Advanced Diuresis
o Refractory diuresis: add metolazone 2.5-5mg (or chlorothiazide 500mg IV) administered 30min before loop diuretic. May need
RHC to clarify hemodynamics or inotropes to augment diuresis. Acetazolamide (500mg daily), as well as dapagliflozin (10mg
daily), may also augment successful decongestion (NEJM 2022;387:1185; EHJ 2023;44:2966). Step-up pharmacologic therapy
superior to RRT in the setting of cardiorenal syndrome (NEJM 2012;367:2296)
o Worsening renal function: Common occurrence. Mild-mod “Cr bumps” likely benign, should not necessarily preclude further
diuresis if pt still congested (Circ 2018;137:2016)
o Endpoints: target resolution of signs/symptoms of congestion. Daily weights, hemoconcentration, lung and JVP POCUS are
useful adjuncts to ensure diuresis to euvolemia. B-lines on lung US portend risk of HF admissions/death (EHJ 2016;37:1244)
• If acute pulmonary edema, NIPPV may improve mortality and reduce need for intubation (Annals 2010;152:590)
• Vasodilators: arterial/venous dilation can relieve symptoms by afterload, PCWP. Consider esp. in severe HTN, acute MR or AR
o Floor: isosorbide dinitrate, hydralazine, nitropaste, captopril; SDU/CCU: nitro gtt, nitroprusside gtt (caution if uncorrected CAD)
• Home GDMT continuation: if not in cardiogenic shock or new AKI, continue ACEi/ARB/ARNi and βB (at fractionated dose) during
ADHF (but do not newly initiate βB) (EHJ 2009;30:2186). Hold SGLT2i as it may preclude procedure
Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)
• HFrEF, HFmrEF (+/- HFimpEF): prioritize initiation of low-dose quadruple GDMT prior to d/c
o Beta-blockers (BB): initiate BB (carvedilol, metoprolol succ., bisoprolol) (COPERNICUS; MERIT-HF). Caution if recent inotropes
o RAAS inhibitors: if renal fxn stable, initiate/titrate ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) (PARADIGM-HF; PIONEER-HF), second line ACEi/ARB
(CONSENSUS; CHARM). Switch to ARNI from ACEi/ARB if no C.I./cost concerns, 36h washout period for ACEi prior to ARNI
o MRA: initiate spironolactone or eplerenone if CrCl>30 (EMPHASIS-HF; RALES). Watch for rebound hyperK after de-escalation of
diuretics (check K, Cr within 72h of discharge)
o SGLT2i: dapaglifozin and empagliflozin reduce mortality and HF admissions regardless of DM (DAPA-HF; EMPEROR-Reduced)
o Guidance for GDMT in advanced CKD: JACC HF 2019;7:371
o GDMT dosing - AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 Guidelines (Circ 2022;145:895)
βB ARNi/ACEi/ARB MRA SGLT2i
metop succ carvedilol sacub/val lisinopril losartan spirono epler dapag empag
Initial Dose (mg) 12.5-25 qD 3.125 BID 49/51 BID 2.5-5 qD 25-50 qD 12.5-25 qD 25 qD 10 qD 10 qD
Target Dose (mg) 200 qD 25-50 BID 97/103 BID 20-40 qD 50-150 qD 25-50 qD 50 qD 10 qD 10 qD
• HFpEF: improve volume overload with diuretics, treat comorbidities (DM, HTN, AF), add GDMT
o SGLT2i found to CV death/hospitalizations in pts with EF >40% (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER)
o Consider spironolactone if normal renal fxn/K, CV death/admits in N/S Am. sites in TOPCAT (Circ 2015;131:34)
o No proven benefit to BB (EHJ 2018;39:26), ACEi (PEP-CHF), ARNi (PARAGON-HF), ARB (CHARM-Preserved; I-PRESERVE)
o New options: finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA) (NEJM 2024;391:1475), semaglutide (GLP1ra) (NEJM 2023;389:2221)
• ICD indicated if: ischemic CM w/ EF ≤30 or ≤35% w/ NYHA II-III; CRT if: EF ≤35% & prolonged QRS ± LBBB & some w/ EF ≤50%
(see Cardiac Devices: PPM/ICD & guidelines for specifics: JACC 2013;61:e6; EHJ 2016;37:2129)
Frederick Lang, Emily Manning
23

panels.title: Source content
panels.text:
Pre-discharge optimization
• Document d/c weight and NTproBNP, appt in HF Transitions Clinic, referral to cardiac rehab
• Optimization of GDMT as above
• Diuretic plan: determine maintenance oral diuretic dose and provide specific instructions for taking additional rescue doses. Consider
inpatient observation on maintenance dose and decide if needs K replacement.

panels.title: CARDIOGENIC SHOCK – CCU
panels.text:
CARDIOGENIC SHOCK – CCU
• Stages: A. “At risk” B. “Beginning”=HDUS pt w/o hypoperfusion (e.g. oliguria, lactate,  Cr.), C. “Classic”=signs of
hypoperfusion (HoTN maybe absent), D. “Deteriorating”=no improvement to initial therapy, E. “Extremis” (JSCAI 2021:1:1)
• Evaluation: ECG, troponin to r/o acute MI. TTE to exclude tamponade/mechanical lesions/contraindications to MCS
• Monitoring: A-line, consider PA catheter for inotropes/pressors and MVO monitoring
2
Immediate Management:
• If c/f acute MI, activate cath lab for PCI (only intervention proven to improve outcomes in cardiogenic shock) (NEJM 1999;341:625)
• ). Escalating inotropes/pressors a/w poor outcomes. Evidence for early initiation of MCS
• Stabilize MAP with norepinephrine PRN prior to obtaining PA catheter to guide tailored therapy
Tailored Therapy: uses invasive hemodynamic monitoring (i.e., PAC) to guide medical therapy. See Pulmonary Artery Catheterization.
• Goals: tissue perfusion (CO, MAP), decongestion (CVP, PCWP), ventricular unloading (minimize myocardial O demand)
2
o Preload: LVEDV ∝ LVEDP  PCWP; goal PCWP 14-18, PAD 16-20, CVP 8-12 → diuresis, UF with RRT
o Afterload: wall stress ∝ MAP (Laplace’s law); SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO; goal MAP >60, SVR <800-1200
▪ Vasodilators: captopril, hydralazine, nitroprusside, TNG, isosorbide dinitrate
▪ Vasopressors: afterload, sometimes needed to MAP in mixed shock or to counteract vasodilatory effect of inodilators
o Contractility: ∝ CO for given preload/afterload; goal CO>4, CI >2.0-2.2, MVO >65
2
▪ Dobutamine (inodilator): β1>β2 agonist (production of cAMP); initial dose 0.5-1 mcg/kg/min
• Watch for tachycardia, ventricular response to AF, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN, tachyphylaxis in infusions >24-48h
▪ Milrinone (inodilator): PDE-3 inhibitor (breakdown of cAMP); initial dose 0.125 mcg/kg/min
• Watch for tachycardia, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN. Compared to dobutamine, milrinone has longer half-life, greater
pulmonary vasodilatation, slightly less chronotropy
• Preferred in patients w/ RV failure. Renally cleared. Often choice for home inotrope for palliative therapy
▪ Epi (inopressor): use if severe HoTN often in combo with inodilators. Watch for arrhythmias, end-organ hypoperfusion
o Advanced: consideration of need for MCS or transplant to improve systemic perfusion; see Mechanical Circulatory Support
Frederick Lang, Emily Manning
24
