lifestyle (salty diet), U = upregulation of cardiac output (e.g. pregnancy, hyperthyroid), R = renal failure, E = embolism. Other triggers:
progression of CM, inadequate diuretic dose, meds (NSAIDs, steroids, CCB, anthracyclines), toxins (EtOH), new/worsened valve
• HF history (prior CM dx, dry weight, last NTproBNP, last TTE/EF, prior ischemic w/u, outpt cardiologist), accurate PAML, social/fam hx
Admission considerations
• Admission orders: tele, 2g Na-restricted diet, daily standing weights, strict I/Os, DVT ppx, (SDU only) electrolyte replenishment scales
• SDU admission indications: EF <25%, NTproBNP ≥ 2,500, arrhythmia-induced HF. Black & Latinx pts w/ HF are less likely to be
admitted to cardiology services, contributing to racial inequities in HF outcomes (Circ Heart Fail 2019;12:e006214)
• Avoid: CCB (esp. non-dihydropyridines), NSAIDs, flecainide
• Check NT-proBNP (& weight) on admission. ADHF unlikely if NT-proBNP <300 (NPV 98%), likely if >450 (>900 if age >50) (Am J
Cardiol 2005;95;948). Difficult to interpret in CKD/dialysis. May be falsely low in obesity, HFpEF
• Screen for and treat iron deficiency in all HF pts independent of Hgb (JACC HF 2019;7:36)
o Dx: ferritin <100 or ferritin <300 + TSat <20% (JACC 2017;70:776)
o Tx: replete with IV iron (JACC 2018;71:782) to sx, functional capacity, and possibly improve outcomes (NEJM 2023;389:975)
Early/acute management
• Diuresis: CVP, PCWP to optimize Starling curve mechanics & relieve sx (NEJM 2017;377:1964; JACC 2020;75:1178)
o Initial tx: IV loop (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide), start w/ 20-40mg IV furosemide if diuretic-naïve otherwise start w/ 2-2.5x
home dose (IV/PO). No difference b/w continuous gtt vs bolus (NEJM 2011;364:797). See Advanced Diuresis
o Refractory diuresis: add metolazone 2.5-5mg (or chlorothiazide 500mg IV) administered 30min before loop diuretic. May need
RHC to clarify hemodynamics or inotropes to augment diuresis. Acetazolamide (500mg daily), as well as dapagliflozin (10mg
daily), may also augment successful decongestion (NEJM 2022;387:1185; EHJ 2023;44:2966). Step-up pharmacologic therapy
superior to RRT in the setting of cardiorenal syndrome (NEJM 2012;367:2296)
o Worsening renal function: Common occurrence. Mild-mod “Cr bumps” likely benign, should not necessarily preclude further
diuresis if pt still congested (Circ 2018;137:2016)
o Endpoints: target resolution of signs/symptoms of congestion. Daily weights, hemoconcentration, lung and JVP POCUS are
useful adjuncts to ensure diuresis to euvolemia. B-lines on lung US portend risk of HF admissions/death (EHJ 2016;37:1244)
• If acute pulmonary edema, NIPPV may improve mortality and reduce need for intubation (Annals 2010;152:590)
• Vasodilators: arterial/venous dilation can relieve symptoms by afterload, PCWP. Consider esp. in severe HTN, acute MR or AR
o Floor: isosorbide dinitrate, hydralazine, nitropaste, captopril; SDU/CCU: nitro gtt, nitroprusside gtt (caution if uncorrected CAD)
• Home GDMT continuation: if not in cardiogenic shock or new AKI, continue ACEi/ARB/ARNi and βB (at fractionated dose) during
ADHF (but do not newly initiate βB) (EHJ 2009;30:2186). Hold SGLT2i as it may preclude procedure
Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)
• HFrEF, HFmrEF (+/- HFimpEF): prioritize initiation of low-dose quadruple GDMT prior to d/c
o Beta-blockers (BB): initiate BB (carvedilol, metoprolol succ., bisoprolol) (COPERNICUS; MERIT-HF). Caution if recent inotropes
o RAAS inhibitors: if renal fxn stable, initiate/titrate ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) (PARADIGM-HF; PIONEER-HF), second line ACEi/ARB
(CONSENSUS; CHARM). Switch to ARNI from ACEi/ARB if no C.I./cost concerns, 36h washout period for ACEi prior to ARNI
o MRA: initiate spironolactone or eplerenone if CrCl>30 (EMPHASIS-HF; RALES). Watch for rebound hyperK after de-escalation of
diuretics (check K, Cr within 72h of discharge)
o SGLT2i: dapaglifozin and empagliflozin reduce mortality and HF admissions regardless of DM (DAPA-HF; EMPEROR-Reduced)
o Guidance for GDMT in advanced CKD: JACC HF 2019;7:371
o GDMT dosing - AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 Guidelines (Circ 2022;145:895)
βB ARNi/ACEi/ARB MRA SGLT2i
metop succ carvedilol sacub/val lisinopril losartan spirono epler dapag empag
Initial Dose (mg) 12.5-25 qD 3.125 BID 49/51 BID 2.5-5 qD 25-50 qD 12.5-25 qD 25 qD 10 qD 10 qD
Target Dose (mg) 200 qD 25-50 BID 97/103 BID 20-40 qD 50-150 qD 25-50 qD 50 qD 10 qD 10 qD
• HFpEF: improve volume overload with diuretics, treat comorbidities (DM, HTN, AF), add GDMT
o SGLT2i found to CV death/hospitalizations in pts with EF >40% (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER)
o Consider spironolactone if normal renal fxn/K, CV death/admits in N/S Am. sites in TOPCAT (Circ 2015;131:34)
o No proven benefit to BB (EHJ 2018;39:26), ACEi (PEP-CHF), ARNi (PARAGON-HF), ARB (CHARM-Preserved; I-PRESERVE)
o New options: finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA) (NEJM 2024;391:1475), semaglutide (GLP1ra) (NEJM 2023;389:2221)
• ICD indicated if: ischemic CM w/ EF ≤30 or ≤35% w/ NYHA II-III; CRT if: EF ≤35% & prolonged QRS ± LBBB & some w/ EF ≤50%
(see Cardiac Devices: PPM/ICD & guidelines for specifics: JACC 2013;61:e6; EHJ 2016;37:2129)
Frederick Lang, Emily Manning
23
Cardiology Heart Failure
Pre-discharge optimization
• Document d/c weight and NTproBNP, appt in HF Transitions Clinic, referral to cardiac rehab
• Optimization of GDMT as above
• Diuretic plan: determine maintenance oral diuretic dose and provide specific instructions for taking additional rescue doses. Consider
inpatient observation on maintenance dose and decide if needs K replacement.
CARDIOGENIC SHOCK – CCU
• Stages: A. “At risk” B. “Beginning”=HDUS pt w/o hypoperfusion (e.g. oliguria, lactate,  Cr.), C. “Classic”=signs of
hypoperfusion (HoTN maybe absent), D. “Deteriorating”=no improvement to initial therapy, E. “Extremis” (JSCAI 2021:1:1)
• Evaluation: ECG, troponin to r/o acute MI. TTE to exclude tamponade/mechanical lesions/contraindications to MCS
• Monitoring: A-line, consider PA catheter for inotropes/pressors and MVO monitoring
2
Immediate Management:
• If c/f acute MI, activate cath lab for PCI (only intervention proven to improve outcomes in cardiogenic shock) (NEJM 1999;341:625)
• ). Escalating inotropes/pressors a/w poor outcomes. Evidence for early initiation of MCS
• Stabilize MAP with norepinephrine PRN prior to obtaining PA catheter to guide tailored therapy
Tailored Therapy: uses invasive hemodynamic monitoring (i.e., PAC) to guide medical therapy. See Pulmonary Artery Catheterization.
• Goals: tissue perfusion (CO, MAP), decongestion (CVP, PCWP), ventricular unloading (minimize myocardial O demand)
2
o Preload: LVEDV ∝ LVEDP  PCWP; goal PCWP 14-18, PAD 16-20, CVP 8-12 → diuresis, UF with RRT
o Afterload: wall stress ∝ MAP (Laplace’s law); SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO; goal MAP >60, SVR <800-1200
▪ Vasodilators: captopril, hydralazine, nitroprusside, TNG, isosorbide dinitrate
▪ Vasopressors: afterload, sometimes needed to MAP in mixed shock or to counteract vasodilatory effect of inodilators
o Contractility: ∝ CO for given preload/afterload; goal CO>4, CI >2.0-2.2, MVO >65
2
▪ Dobutamine (inodilator): β1>β2 agonist (production of cAMP); initial dose 0.5-1 mcg/kg/min
• Watch for tachycardia, ventricular response to AF, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN, tachyphylaxis in infusions >24-48h
▪ Milrinone (inodilator): PDE-3 inhibitor (breakdown of cAMP); initial dose 0.125 mcg/kg/min
• Watch for tachycardia, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN. Compared to dobutamine, milrinone has longer half-life, greater
pulmonary vasodilatation, slightly less chronotropy
• Preferred in patients w/ RV failure. Renally cleared. Often choice for home inotrope for palliative therapy
▪ Epi (inopressor): use if severe HoTN often in combo with inodilators. Watch for arrhythmias, end-organ hypoperfusion
o Advanced: consideration of need for MCS or transplant to improve systemic perfusion; see Mechanical Circulatory Support

topics.title: Right Ventricular Failure

panels.title: PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGIES (NEJM 2023;388:1111)
panels.text:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGIES (NEJM 2023;388:1111)
• Normal RV function: governed by systemic venous return, PA pressure, pericardial
RV “death spiral”
compliance, and native contractility of the RV free wall and interventricular septum
(where RV and LV are “tethered”)
o The RV is coupled to the high-compliance, low-resistance pulm circulation 
RV ejects blood at lower pressure compared to LV  RV is more afterload
sensitive than LV. RV can adapt to changes in volume > pressure.
• Acute RV Failure: RV & LV interdependent  failure of RV  failure of LV via: (1)
decreased LV preload, as RV output = LV preload & (2) septal bowing into LV,
causing diastolic impairment (“Diastolic Ventricular Interaction”)
o RV afterload (e.g. PE, hypoxemia, acidemia), RV preload (e.g. LR shunt
or TV disease), or RV contractility (e.g. MI, myocarditis) all lead to increased
RV wall stress & resultant ischemia -> “death spiral”
• Chronic RV Failure: gradual RV afterload (e.g. from pulmonary hypertension /
pulmonic stenosis / tricuspid regurgitation) Eur Heart J 2020;41:543

panels.title: CLINICAL FEATURES AND WORKUP (Circ 2018;137:e578-e622)
panels.text:
CLINICAL FEATURES AND WORKUP (Circ 2018;137:e578-e622)
• Exam: JVP, Kussmaul’s sign (JVP with inspiration), peripheral edema, RV heave, pulsatile liver, split S2, new TR murmur
• EKG: RAD, R:S amplitude >1 in V1, p-wave > 2.5mm in inferior leads (P pulmonale), S1Q3T3 (RV strain in PE), atrial arrhythmias
• Labs: NT-proBNP, troponin, also Cr and LFTs secondary to venous congestion (LFTs may be normal in chronic RV failure)
• Imaging: PA/lateral CXR; chest CT  RV/LV ratio >0.9 suggests RV strain
• Echo: measure RV size/fxn/pressure to elucidate etiology. Aortic root, LA, RV should be ~1:1:1 in size (PSL view). RV should be < LV
in size (Apical 4Ch view). RVEF based on displacement of base towards apex, correlates with TAPSE = tricuspid annular plane
systolic excursion (normal ≥ 17 mm; reflects apex-to-base shortening). RVSP calculated from TR jet, correlates w/ RHC but can vary
within 10mmHg (esp w/ lung disease, PPV)
• RHC w/ placement of PA line: gold standard for measurement of ventricular filling pressures, CO, PA pressures
o Assessments of RV function – CVP/PCWP ratio: normal = 0.5,  is sign of RV dysfunction; PAPi: (PAs – PAd)/CVP <0.9 = RV
failure, for pts w/ VAD < 1.85 = RV failure; RV stroke work index: (mPAP – CVP) x (CI/HR) x 0.0136 (normal 8-12 g/m/beat/m2)

panels.title: MANAGEMENT (Circ 2018;137:e578)
panels.text:
MANAGEMENT (Circ 2018;137:e578)
• Treat reversible causes (e.g. pericardial disease, RVMI, PE, hypoxemia, infections)
• Preload (CVP goal 8-12mmHg): both hypo- and hypervolemia can CO
o Volume responsive (PE, RVMI): judicious IVF (0.5-1L) in absence of CVP elevation (goal CVP 10-14 in RVMI)
o Volume overload: IV diuresis to RV pressures, functional TR, and improve LV CO; consider CRRT if refractory to diuresis
• Afterload:
o Systemic: if pt hypotensive, start pressors – do not tolerate HoTN as propagates RV death spiral (CPP); Goal MAP>65 &
MAP>mPAP (EHJ Acute CV Care 2022;11:77) no clinical data regarding pressor of choice, but often choose vasopressin or
norepinephrine (vaso affects PVR less than norepi) (Crit Care Med 2007;35:2037)
o Pulmonary: remove factors that pulm vasc tone (e.g. hypoxemia, acidemia). Consider pulm vasodilators if evidence of PAH
(inhaled>oral to deliver vasodilators to ventilated vascular beds)
▪ Types: iNO, prostacyclin agonists (epoprostenol (Veletri), inhaled or IV), endothelin antagonists (e.g. bosentan,
ambrisentan), nitric oxide enhancers (e.g. PDE-5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil)
• Contractility: milrinone (RV afterload by pulm vasodilation but HoTN risk); epinephrine (RV contractility, MAP). In RVMI,
important to revascularize urgently as inotropes can exacerbate ischemia.
• Devices: if refractory RVF, consider RV MCS and/or biventricular support (ProtekDuo, Impella RP, VA-ECMO)

panels.title: INTUBATION AND MECHANICAL VENTILATION (Curr Heart Fail Rep 2012;9:228)
panels.text:
INTUBATION AND MECHANICAL VENTILATION (Curr Heart Fail Rep 2012;9:228)
• RV preload is “extrathoracic” and afterload is “intrathoracic” → intubation/PPV  PVR & RV afterload→ RV dilation→“death spiral”
• Mech vent/NIPPV in RV failure precipitate risk for hemodynamic collapse & cardiac arrest; trial of HFNC for hypoxemic respiratory
failure preferred prior to MV/NIPPV given minimal effect on RV afterload.
o Drugs commonly used in intubation (BZDs, propofol, muscle relaxants)  tendency towards vasodilation and negative inotropy
decreased venous return  decreased RV/LV preload  systemic hypoTN  propagates “death spiral”
o Consider rapid sequence intubation w/ hemodynamically stable induction agents (ketamine/etomidate >> propofol for induction)
& push dose epinephrine (5-20mcg) or phenylephrine if emergent intubation; have norepi in line anticipating hypotension.
• Vent management: prevent hypoxemia & hypercarbia (PVR), consider moderate TV (~8cc/kg), low PEEP (<8 cm H O), and
2
moderate plateau pressure goal (<30 mmHg) to help minimize RV afterload

panels.title: RIGHT VENTRICULAR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (ACC/AHA: Circ 2013;127:e362)
panels.text:
RIGHT VENTRICULAR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (ACC/AHA: Circ 2013;127:e362)
• EKG: check R-sided ECG leads in pts with inferior STEMI (10-15% have RV involvement)
o 1mm STE in V4R  88% Sn, 78% Sp in inferior STEMI; STE III>II suggests RCA > LCx and RVMI
o High-grade AV block seen in ~50% of pts with RVMI
• Management: pts with RVMI may initially benefit from fluid bolus; caution w/ TNG (preload) & BB
Frederick Lang

INDICATIONS FOR HEART TRANSPLANT (CURR OPIN NEPHROL HYPERTENS 2025;34:16)
Advanced HF refractory to therapy, defined as: (1) cardiogenic shock requiring inotrope or MCS, or (2) NYHA class IV sx refractory to
maximal therapy alongside low HF prognosis score or poor CPET results, or (3) refractory life-threatening arrhythmias

topics.title: Pulmonary Artery Catheterization

panels.title: OVERVIEW
panels.text:
OVERVIEW
• Indications: PA catheter (PAC) for tailored therapy; diagnose (1) undifferentiated shock (2) cardiogenic vs. non-cardiogenic pulm edema;
(3) LV vs RV failure; (4) etiology of PH; (5) L R shunting; (6) valve disease; (7) pericardial
disease
• Efficacy: controversial - ESCAPE trial (JAMA 2005;294:1625) showed no mortality benefit to empiric
use of PAC in pts w/ ADHF off inotropes. Recent observational study (JACC Heart Fail 2020:8:11)
mortality benefit for cardiogenic shock. PACs are still guideline-recommended in carefully selected
patients (e.g. pts w/ MCS) (Circulation 2022;145:e895)
• Line course: central vein (IJ/fem)SVC/IVCRARVPAdistal pulmonary arteriole
VENOUS WAVEFORMS (CVP/PCWP)
• a wave: atrial contraction; coincides with the QRS complex (on CVP tracing)
• c wave: bowing of TV into atrium during ventricular contraction; more visible in 1st degree AVB
• x descent: atrial relaxation (early x descent), downward movement of TV (late x descent)
• v wave: passive atrial filling (venous return) when TV/MV closed; coincides with T wave
• y descent: rapid atrial emptying following opening of the TV (ventricular diastole)
• Sample waveforms available in J Clin Monit Comput 2022;36:5

panels.title: OBTAINING PA LINE NUMBERS ON AM ROUNDS
panels.text:
OBTAINING PA LINE NUMBERS ON AM ROUNDS
1) Position patient supine with head-of-bed between 0-60°
2) Align transducer with mid-axillary line (4th intercostal space)
3) Zero transducer to air & assess waveform for dampness
4) Record PA systolic, PA diastolic, PA mean, CVP, & line position
5) Open the PA catheter balloon port & remove 1.5cc air
6) Inject 1.5cc air slowly until PCWP waveform observed (use minimum air required to  risk of PA
infarction/rupture) & record PCWP (limit balloon inflation <10 seconds)
7) Release safety syringe & allow balloon to deflate passively; verify balloon deflated by visualizing
the PA waveform
8) Troubleshooting: CXR to evaluate position (obtained daily)
a. Arrhythmia: catheter may be in RVOT; consider repositioning
b. Dampened waveform: kinked tubing, air/thrombus, or catheter tip against vessel wall; flush
and/or withdraw catheter
c. No PCWP tracing: catheter tip is not far enough, balloon has ruptured, or catheter is coiled in
RV
d. Continuous PCWP: catheter tip is advanced too far (“overwedged”)
e. mvO2 resembles arterial O2: catheter tip is advanced too far
CALCULATING HEMODYNAMIC PARAMETERS
• Normal: “rule of 5s”  RA 5, RV 25/5, PA 25/10, PCWP 10, LV 125/10
• Cardiac output: TD better predicts mortality (JAMA Cardiol 2017:10:10)
o Fick = VO2 / (13.4 * Hgb * [SpO2 – MvO2]) [nml: 4-8 L/min]
▪ VO2  250 ml/min OR 3*wt(kg) OR 125*BSA
o Thermodilution (TD): temp change (measured by thermistor) is proportional to LV CO
(inaccurate if: severe TR, intracardiac shunt, very low CO)
• Cardiac index = CO/BSA [nl: 2.2-4.2 L/min/m2] (nl  w/ age)
• SVR = (MAP-CVP) / CO x 80 [nl: 700-1200 dynes*s*cm5]
• PVR = (mPAP-PCWP) / CO [nl: <2 Woods units]
• PAPi = (PASP – PADP) / RAP [PAPi < 0.9  severe RV dysfxn]

panels.title: HEMODYNAMIC CONSIDERATIONS
panels.text:
HEMODYNAMIC CONSIDERATIONS
• All quantitative pressure measurements (especially PCWP) should be made at end-expiration (when intrathoracic pressure is zero)
o Spontaneous respiration: RA & PCWP  with expiration  measure from the higher a waves (“patient = peak”)
o Positive pressure ventilation: RA & PCWP  with expiration  measure from the lower a waves (“vent = valley”)
• Measure RA & PCWP at end-diastole (i.e. just before the c wave)
• Correlate PCWP with PA diastolic pressure; if well correlated, can trend PAd as proxy for PCWP (allowing for less frequent wedging)

panels.title: CLINICAL CONSIDERATIONS
panels.text:
CLINICAL CONSIDERATIONS
• Placement: usually through RIJ Cordis. Advance ONLY with balloon inflated. Deflate balloon when withdrawing and at ALL other times.
.
o Cath lab if: severe PH (>70mmHg), large RV/RA, LBBB, PPM/ICD <6mo, temp wire, severe TR, prosthetic TV/PV, femoral access
• Contraindications: absolute – insertion site infection, RVAD, RA/RV mass/thrombosis, mechanical TV/PV, endocarditis (TV/PV)
• Position: on CXR, should be in middle 1/3 of the chest bilaterally; ability to wedge more important than CXR position
• Complications: infection, bleeding, thrombosis, PTX, arrythmia (PVC, NSVT, VT), RBBB, CHB, valve trauma, PA rupture (place patient on
side with the catheter “bleeding side down”, order STAT CXR, CBC, coags, CT surgery consult), RV perforation, pulm infarct, PE, catheter
knotting (difficult removal), balloon rupture & embolization
Lianet Vazquez
27

panels.title: PHYSIOLOGICAL PACING (CPP), & CARDIAC CONTRACTILITY MODULATION (CCM)
panels.text:
PHYSIOLOGICAL PACING (CPP), & CARDIAC CONTRACTILITY MODULATION (CCM)
• Types: single chamber (RA or RV lead), dual chamber (RA + RV leads), biventricular (RV + coronary sinus ± RA leads)
• PPM: sense/pace the RA & RV to treat bradyarrhythmias (see tables for nomenclature and common modes)
• ICD: device with an RV lead capable of terminating ventricular arrhythmias via anti-tachycardia pacing, cardioversion, or defibrillation
o CPP: any form of cardiac pacing intended to restore/preserve synchrony of ventricular contraction, including: Cardiac Resynchronization
Therapy (CRT): provides simultaneous RV + LV pacing in HFrEF pts w/ wide QRS to desynchrony → LV reverse remodeling & LVEF
o Conduction System Pacing (CSP): recruitment of intrinsic conduction system by either His bundle pacing or LBB area pacing
• CCM: delivers biphasic electric stimulation to the ventricular myocardium during absolute refractory period to augment LV contraction
o CRT-P = BiV ± RA pacing; CRT-D = CRT-P w/ ICD function

topics.title: Valvular Heart Disease

panels.title: AORTIC STENOSIS
panels.text:
AORTIC STENOSIS
• Etiology: degenerative calcific AS (age-related; precursor is aortic sclerosis; most common cause >70yo), bicuspid valve (most
common cause <70yo), rheumatic heart disease (RHD; often w/ leaflet fusion, concurrent MV dz), radiation
• Clinical Manifestations: most important determinant of prognosis = sxs: 50% mortality at 5y if angina, 3y if syncope, 2y if HF
o Angina: afterload  LV pressures  LVH  O2 demand  supply-demand mismatch w/ exertion or tachycardia
o Syncope: caused by exercise-induced vasodilation w/ fixed ability to augment CO due to stenosis
o Heart failure (dyspnea): LVH  diastolic dysfunction (systolic dysfunction is a late finding)
o Acquired vWF def: 20% of severe AS, can worsen bleeding from GI AVMs “Heyde syndrome” (NEJM 2012;367:1954)
• Diagnosis:
o Physical exam: harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at RUSB radiating to carotids. Signs of severe AS: late-peaking murmur
(long ejection time), delayed carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus), soft or paradoxical split S2, diminished murmur (low flow)
o TTE: measure mean (not peak) gradient, valve area, & peak jet velocity; assess EF as ↓ flow ↓ gradient confounds severity
• Severe AS: peak AV velocity ≥4m/s, mean AV pressure grad ≥40mmHg, or AV area (AVA) ≤1cm2 (ACC/AHA: Circ 2021;143:e35)
o ECG: LVH, LAE, LAFB, LBBB
o Exercise stress testing: recommended in asymptomatic severe AS to assess for symptoms; do not perform in pts w/ sx
o Low-flow/low-gradient AS: severity underestimated in reduced EF as ↓ flow ↓ gradient. Subsets distinguished by flow (low-
flow: SVi <35 mL/m2), gradient (low-gradient: <40mmHg), LVEF, and dobutamine stress TTE (DSE) (Circ 2011;124:739)
▪ True LF/LG AS: low EF, flow, & gradient; confirm w/ DSE V
max
>4m/s or gradient>40mmHg w/ AVA<1cm2; poor outcomes
▪ Pseudosevere AS: a normal valve w/ low measured AVA in the setting of low EF; due to flow-dependent AVA estimation
and decreased ability of weakened ventricle to fully open aortic valve; confirm w/ DSE with improved AVA >1cm2
▪ Paradoxical LF/LG AS: preserved EF, yet low-flow and low-gradient; poor outcomes (Circulation 2013;128:1781)
• Natural History: highly variable, but on average, AVA  ~0.1 cm2/yr & mean gradient 8mmHg/yr (JACC 1989;13:545). Patients with
bicuspid valves, advanced age, & those with severe leaflet calcification are at risk for more rapid progression
• Aortic Valve Replacement (AVR) (J Am Soc Echo 2018;31:117): indications based on: symptoms, severity (TTE criteria), LVEF
o Symptomatic, severe AS (Stage D): prompt AVR indicated due to risk of sudden death
o Asymptomatic, severe AS (Stage C): AVR appropriate if: LVEF<50%; symptoms provoked with exercise testing; or undergoing
other cardiac surgery. For patients with asymptomatic very severe AS (AVA ≤0.75cm2), early surgery may have mortality benefit
(NEJM 2020;382:111). For asymptomatic severe AS, early TAVR may reduce unplanned CV hospitalization (EARLY TAVR).
o Low-flow, low-gradient AS: true LF/LG = AVR indicated, paradoxical = AVR if symptomatic, pseudosevere = AVR not indicated
o Bioprosthetic vs Mechanical: if contraindications to AC with VKA, must offer bioprosthetic; if pt <50 years of age without
contraindications to AC, SAVR w/ mechanical valve recommended (COR 1; Circulation 2021;143:35); if >65 yrs of age,
bioprosthetic recommended (COR 2a); 50-65 years of age require shared decision making
o SAVR vs TAVR for bioprosthetic: pts <65yr, SAVR recommended d/t increased durability; >80yr TAVR recommended
o 65-80 yrs of age: depends on surgical risk (STS-PROM score), concomitant heart/vascular disease, valvular/vascular
anatomy that is amenable to TAVR (Circulation 2021;143:35)
o TAVR is recommended for those at extreme surgical risk (compared to medical therapy, PARTNER); noninferior to
SAVR in those at high (NEJM 2011;364:2187), intermediate (PARTNER 2), & low surgical risk (PARTNER 3). Valve-in-
valve TAVR may additionally be beneficial in pts with surgical bioprosthetic AV failure (JACC 2017;69:2253)
o TAVR Evaluation: c/s structural cardiology, cardiac surgery. Obtain TTE, TAVR-protocol CT, dental clearance (Panorex)
o TAVR Complications: Valve: embolization, paravalvular leak; Stroke: embolic (first 48h), ischemic/hemorrhagic; Conduction:
HAVB requiring PPM (Major RF: baseline RBBB, need for pacing or HAVB s/p TAVR; Minor: h/o AF, valve oversized >15%;
Card Fail Rev 2021; 7:e12); Bleeding; Access site complication; Hemodynamics: dynamic LVOT obstruction due to LVH (“suicide
LV”), HTN (sudden ↓ in obstruction after TAVR), hypotension (d/t ↓preload), tamponade (perforation, usually immediate); AKI
• Medical Management: AS is a surgical disease & medical management is only utilized for treatment of sx
o Treat HTN: reduce the “double load” on the ventricle. In theory, ACE-I beneficial for LV fibrosis; however, no optimal regimen
exists because anti-hypertensives can lead to hemodynamic issues. Bottom line: start low and go slow
o Control volume status: operate within a narrow preload range, prone to underfilling (low preload) & overfilling (volume overload)
• Anticoagulation after Valve Replacement:
o Bridging UFH or LMWH if AC interrupted only in mechanical MV or mechanical AV with RFs (Class I),
o RFs: AF, LV dysfxn, prior VTE, hypercoag, older generaction mechanical AVR (Circ 2021;143:e35)
o Bleeding risk: mechanical > bioprosthetic (likely AC related). Reoperation risk: bioprosthetic > mechanical
o TAVR: ASA monotherapy non-inferior to DAPT for thrombotic events & associated with less bleeding (NEJM 2020;383:1447)

>3 months after placement ASA 81 IIa

panels.title: AORTIC REGURGITATION (AKA INSUFFICIENCY)
panels.text:
AORTIC REGURGITATION (AKA INSUFFICIENCY)
• Etiology: Acute: IE, aortic dissection, traumatic, prosthetic valve failure; Chronic: primary valve disease (bicuspid valve, endocarditis,
RHD, CTD, myxomatous degeneration) or secondary root dilation (in aortic aneurysm due to HTN, CTD, syphilis)
• Pathophysiology: Acute: diastolic regurgitant flow  sudden LVEDP (w/o remodeling time)  CO  pulmonary edema; Chronic:
diastolic regurgitant flow  LVEDP  initial maintenance of SV/CO  progressive ventricular dilatation  LV failure
• Clinical/Exam: angina, L-sided HF. Acute: cardiogenic shock. Chronic: pulse pressure (bounding pulses, bouncing head/uvula, nail
bed capillary pulse; Int J Card 2006;107:421)
o Auscultation: high-pitched, blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur along LSB. Longer murmur = more severe/chronic. May hear
low-pitched diastolic murmur at apex secondary to regurgitant jet displacing anterior mitral leaflet (“Austin Flint murmur”)
• Treatment:
o Acute: usually needs surgery. Nitroprusside to afterload; ino- and chronotrocpes to diastolic time. Do not use
vasoconstrictors or IABP (which worsen regurg) or beta-blockers (which block compensation and diastolic regurgitant time)
o Chronic: ACEi/ARB/ARNI first line, CCB or hydralazine/nitrates 2nd line to reduce LV afterload. AV replacement if: severe AR
AND symptomatic, LVEF<55%, LV end-systolic dimension >50mm, or undergoing other cardiac surgery (JACC 2021;77:e25)

panels.title: MITRAL STENOSIS
panels.text:
MITRAL STENOSIS
• Etiology: RHD (~80% of MS; only 50-70% report h/o rheumatic fever), IE, annular calcification, congenital, autoimmune valvulitis
(SLE, RA), carcinoid syndrome, endomyocardial fibroelastosis, radiation (e.g., 10-20y after Hodgkin’s tx)
• Pathophysiology: elevated LAP  pHTN, AFib (47%). Demand for CO precipitates symptoms. Valve narrows ~0.1cm2/y
• Clinical/Exam: dyspnea (most common), pulmonary edema, hemoptysis, VTE even w/o AFib (Am Heart J 2000; 140:658), RV failure
o Auscultation: loud S1, high-pitched opening snap (more severe if earlier, indicating higher LAP); low-pitched diastolic rumble
• Treatment: Medical: warfarin if LA thrombus, AFib, prior embolism (Class I) or LA > 55mm (Class IIb). Beta-blockers if tachycardic or
dyspneic, diuresis if pulm edema. If rheumatic, secondary ppx against strep as below (Circulation 2021;143:e35)
o Intervention: generally, need to have severe MS (MV area 1cm2) + symptoms to be considered for intervention
▪ Rheumatic MS: symptomatic pts with severe rheumatic MS and favorable valve morphology (based on TTE, Wilkins Score)
→Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC). Consider PMBC if asymptomatic AND elevated pulmonary
pressures (>50mmHg; COR 2a) or new AF (COR 2b). Proceed to surgical MVR if: severe symptomatic MS AND either not
PBMC candidate, PBMC fails, or undergoing another cardiac surgery (JACC 2021;77:e25)
▪ Nonrheumatic Calcific MS: because calcification involves the annulus and base of the leaflets without commissural fusion,
there is no role for PMBC or surgical commissurotomy; consider MVR only after discussion of high risk (COR 2b)

panels.title: MITRAL REGURGITATION
panels.text:
MITRAL REGURGITATION
• Etiology: Acute: ischemic (often inferior MI), IE, traumatic, spontaneous chordal rupture; Chronic: primary (MVP, ischemic,
degenerative, RHD, IE, CTD) or secondary (“functional MR”: dilated LV/annulus in dilated CM, systolic anterior motion in HCM)
• Pathophysiology: LA/LV volume overload  LV dysfxn, progressive enlargement of LV  dilated mitral annulus  regurgitation
• Clinical: Acute: flash pulmonary edema, hypotension, shock; Chronic: DOE, orthopnea, PND, AFib, pulmonary  periph edema
• Exam: holosystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla, S3, displaced PMI. If acute: early diastolic rumble and S3 may be only signs
• Treatment:
o Acute: afterload, inotropes (dobutamine), diuresis. If hemodynamically unstable (esp. post-MI or endocarditis), consider IABP
and/or urgent surgical repair (NEJM 2012;366:2466). If ischemic, consider revascularization
o Chronic: GDMT for HF if applicable
▪ Severe primary MR: symptomatic w/ any EF OR asymptomatic w/ EF  60% or LVESD  40mm → MVR (Circulation
2021;143:e35); primary MR w/ high surgical risk, transcatheter edge to edge repair (M-TEER) (COR 2a; EVEREST II).
▪ Severe “functional MR”: if LVEF 50% OR unfavorable anatomy AND symptomatic on maximal GDMT OR undergoing
CABG → MVR; if LVEF <50% AND persistent symptoms on maximal GDMT AND anatomy favorable → M-TEER (COAPT).

panels.title: TRICUSPID REGURGITATION
panels.text:
TRICUSPID REGURGITATION
• Etiology: Primary: IE, RHD, iatrogenic (device leads, etc), congenital, trauma, carcinoid, drugs, ischemic papillary muscle
dysfunction; Secondary: dilated RV in pulm HTN, dilated CM, RV volume overload; dilated annulus (associated w/ AF)
• Pathophysiology: similar to mitral regurgitation, but involving RA/RV and tricuspid annulus
• Clinical: Right-sided heart failure: hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema, large V in JVP, pulsatile liver, substernal pulsation
o Ausculation: holosystolic murmur at left mid- or lower- sternal border that increases with inspiration, S3
• Treatment: Medical: Diuresis (COR 2a), management of underlying cause
o Tricuspid valve replacement if: (1) severe TR undergoing left-sided valve surgery; (2) symptomatic (i.e., with R heart failure)
primary severe TR; (3) symptomatic secondary severe TR poorly responsive to GDMT without ↑PAP or left HF (4) progressive
TR if undergoing L valve surgery AND either tricuspid annular dilation >4 cm or R heart failure (5) consider in asymptomatic
primary severe TR with progressive RV dilation / systolic dysfunction (JACC 2021;77:e25)
o Transcatheter therapies (T-TEER) are emerging which may ↓ TR severity and ↑ QoL in severe TR (NEJM 2023;388:1833)

panels.title: GENERAL PRINCIPLES
panels.text:
GENERAL PRINCIPLES
• Rheumatic Disease: secondary ppx against streptococcus recommended for 10yr or until 40 yrs old (whichever longer, COR I)
• AF and Valvular disease: w/o mechanical valve, DOAC reasonable VKA except in rheumatic MS, practice variable for nonrheum MS
• IE Prophylaxis: Reasonable in pts undergoing high-risk dental manipulation with 1) prosthetic valves, 2) prosthetic material used in
valve repair, 3) prior IE, 4) CHD unrepaired or incompletely repaired, 5) s/p cardiac transplant with valvulopathy, 6) CHD completely
repaired with prosthetic material for 1st 6 months post-op (COR 2a; Circulation 2021; 143:35)
Joseph Replogle

topics.title: Pericardial Disease

panels.title: CARDIAC TAMPONADE
panels.text:
CARDIAC TAMPONADE
• Definition: hemodynamic insufficiency caused by impaired cardiac filling due to pericardial pressure due to effusion, leading to
intracardiac chamber pressures & eventually equalization of diastolic pressure in all 4 heart chambers
• Etiologies of pericardial effusion: idiopathic (20%), iatrogenic (16%), malignant (13%), uremic, infectious, HF, autoimmune (Am J Med
2000;109:95). Tamponade more likely in malignant, post-viral (including SARS-CoV-2), uremic, iatrogenic (i.e. post-cath) etiologies. Also
seen with prox. aortic dissection & myocardial wall rupture
Clinical Manifestation and Diagnosis:
• Beck’s Triad: BP, JVP, muffled heart sounds; elevated BP does not rule out
• Pulsus paradoxus (PP): exaggeration of normal decrease in SBP during inspiration (If >10mmHg, LR=3.3. If ≤10 mmHg, LR=0.03)
1. Slowly deflate BP cuffnote pressure when systolic Korotkoff sounds only heard during expiration (will sound irregular) (a)
 continue slowly deflating BP cuff until Korotkoff sounds heard throughout; (b) PP = a – b
2. Via A-line tracing (PP = height exp. – height insp. systolic waveform)
• ECG: sinus tach, low QRS voltage (50%; limb ≤5mm, precordial ≤10mm), electrical alternans (20%; precordial leads)
• TTE: inspiratory leftward septal shift, diastolic collapse of cardiac chambers (R > L-sided), respirophasic changes in transvalvular
velocities, IVC plethora. SIZE of effusion does NOT predict tamponade – RATE of accumulation is more important
Treatment:
• Fluid resuscitation: administer volume urgently to increase intracardiac pressures (monitor closely as overfilling can worsen
tamponade), starting w/ 250-500cc bolus; greatest benefit for SBP < 100 mmHg (Circ 2008;117:1545). Inotrope if needed. Avoid BB
• PPV: avoid if possible as positive intrathoracic pressure will further impede ventricular filling
• Drainage: catheter pericardiocentesis, surgical pericardiectomy (if aortic/myocardial rupture), or HD (if uremic)
o Analysis of pericardial fluid: cell count, total protein, LDH, gram stain/cx, fungal or AFB smear/cx (if relevant), ADA/IFN-
gamma/lysozyme (if concerned for TB), cytology/tumor markers
o Removal of drain: when output <50cc/d, otherwise consider pericardial window (pleural>abdominal). See Pericardial Drain
PERICARDITIS
ECG Evolution in Pericarditis (JACC 2020;75:76)
• Classification: acute (<6w), incessant (>6w w/o remission), recurrent (return
after symptom-free interval of 4-6 wks), chronic (>3months)
• Epidemiology: 5% ED pts w/ non-ischemic chest pain, M > F, young > elderly

• Hospitalize if: fever, WBC, large effusion (>2cm), immunosuppressed, anticoagulated, trauma, troponin, unstable/signs of
tamponade, failure to respond to NSAIDs after 7d. Also consider hospitalization if subacute presentation
• 1st-line treatment: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen 600-800mg TID; ASA 650-975 TID; indomethacin 25-50mg TID) ± colchicine 0.6mg BID
(qd if pt <70kg) + PPI in select pts for GI ppx (hx PUD, age>65, concomitant anticoagulation/steroid)
o ASA: preferred over NSAIDs if: post-MI, CKD (GFR <45), concomitant anti-platelet/anticoagulant therapy
o Activity restriction: avoid strenuous activity until symptom resolution
• Glucocorticoids (prednisone 0.25-0.5mg/kg/d): preferred over NSAIDs if: sx refractory to 7d of NSAID treatment, recurrent (>2
episodes), uremic pericarditis, CTD pericarditis, or contraindication to NSAIDs. Associated w/ recurrence if first idiopathic episode
due to flares during weaning. Duration: NSAIDs: until sx resolve (1-2w), then taper (total 3-4w). Colchicine: 3mo (no taper).
Glucocorticoids: 2w, then taper (2-4 mo total)
Recurrent pericarditis
• Treatment: generally same as initial episode but longer wean (colchicine for 6+ months and wean NSAID by CRP trend)
• Consider IL-1 inhibitors (NEJM 2021;384:31)
• .

• Clinical presentation of constrictive pericarditis can mimic decompensated heart failure or volume overload
• Definitive treatment is pericardiectomy + treatment of underlying cause

panels.title: ACUTE AORTIC SYNDROMES (AAS) (Nat Rev Cardiol 2015;12:103)(Lancet 2023;401;p773)
panels.text:
ACUTE AORTIC SYNDROMES (AAS) (Nat Rev Cardiol 2015;12:103)(Lancet 2023;401;p773)
Source: UpToDate
Etiology: five distinct processes with risk of rupture
• Class I: Classic dissection (intimal tear resulting in a false lumen)
• Class II: Intramural hematoma (IMH, rupture of vasa vasorum causing
hematoma within aortic wall without tear)
Source: UpToDate
• Class III: Limited dissection (limited intimal tear without dissection) Location:
• Class IV: Atherosclerotic ulcer (PAU, penetrating adventitia with DeBakey: type I (ascending+descending); type II
surrounding hematoma) (ascending only); type III (descending only)
• Class V: Iatrogenic/traumatic Stanford: type A (ascendingdescending); type B
(descending)
Epidemiology:
• Prevalence: aortic dissection most common (62-88%), followed by IMH (10-30%) & penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (PAU) (2-8%)
• Risk factors: male, HTN, age 60-70 (if <40yo, think Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos type IV, CTD, bicuspid valve), atherosclerosis,
prior cardiac surgery, aortic aneurysm, FHx of AAS, aortitis, trauma, pregnancy
• Aortic dissection prognosis:
o Type A: mortality at 3y among patients discharged alive: Medical: 31%, Surgical: 10% (Circ 2006;114:I350)
o Type B: Medical: 8% in-hospital mortality, 15% 1y, 24% 3y, 57% 10y (J Vasc Surg 2021;73:48)
• IMH will progress to complete dissection in 28-47% of cases. PAU will progress to aortic rupture in 42%.
Diagnosis:
• Clinical features: AD, IMH, & PAU cannot be distinguished by presentation alone
o Signs: AI murmur, pulse deficit, upper extremity BP differential (>20mmHg), decompensated heart failure
o Sx: chest or back pain (radiates to neck/jaw if ascending; back/abdomen if descending; may migrate as dissection propagates)
• Complications: syncope, shock, malperfusion syndrome secondary to branch artery occlusion (MI, stroke, paraplegia, limb
ischemia, renal failure); aortic valve regurgitation, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade
• Risk Score: Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS): d-dimer versus directly to CTA (Circ 2018;3;250) and AORTA
simplified score (AORTAs): increased sensitivity, decreased sensitivity (JAHA 2021;10:3)
• Labs: rule out if D-dimer <500ng/mL (96% NPV), troponin (can be  if dissection extends into coronaries)
• Imaging:
CXR -50% with AAS have normal CXR; only 1/3 will have widened mediastinum
-Sn 95%, Sp 87-100%; first-line modality in pts w/ high clinical probability of AAS
CT-A
-Combined I+/I- (assess for IMH, mediastinum hemorrhage, or hemopericardium)
-Sn 73-100%, Sp 71-91%, least accurate of diagnostic imaging modalities
TTE
-Useful for identifying AV dysfunction, prox dissections extending to Ao root/pericardium
-Sn 99%, Sp 90-100%. Often used intra-op to confirm dx prior to surgery
TEE
-Invasive nature limits use; cannot detect pathology below the diaphragm
Management:
• Goal: “impulse control”  minimize aortic wall stress by LV ejection force (dP/dT): goal HR 60-80 SBP <120mmHg
• Agents:
o IV beta blockade (esmolol, labetalol); except if acute severe AI or other contraindication.
o If additional BP control required: IV nitroprusside, TNG, nicardipine. If refractory HTN, consider renal artery involvement.
▪ NEVER use vasodilators for AA without AI without concomitant beta blockade  will increase wall stress via reflex
tachycardia, thereby increasing dP/dT. Opiate analgesia attenuates release of catecholamines (Lancet 2015;385:800)
• Urgent surgical consultation (CT surgery)
• Aortic Dissection:
o Type A: immediate open surgical repair 26% mortality vs >50% with medical management (JAMA 2000;283:897)
o Type B: uncomplicated: medical therapy (80% survival at 5y); complicated (compromise of renal/mesenteric vessels): TEVAR.
However, INSTEAD-XL showed improved outcomes with low-risk preemptive TEVAR in all Type B dissections
• IMH & PAU: Type A: urgent (i.e., within days) open surgical repair vs. Type B: medical management or TEVAR
Daniel Weiner, Rachel Wittenberg
32

topics.title: Syncope

panels.title: OVERVIEW
panels.text:
OVERVIEW
• Definition: transient (self-limited) loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion that is associated with loss of postural tone,
followed by complete spontaneous recovery; excludes metabolic causes (e.g. hypoglycemia, hypoxia, intoxication)
• Risk assessment and need for hospitalization:
o High-risk symptoms: preceding palpitations, exertional syncope, bleeding, syncope while supine, lack of prodrome, trauma
o High-risk features: angina, CHF, mod-severe valvular or structural heart disease, ECG features of ischemia/arrhythmia, FHx of
SCD, preexcitation syndromes, high-risk occupation (e.g. airline pilot), facial trauma (lack of warning time)
o Risk calculators have high NPV (>95%) but do NOT replace clinical judgment
▪ San Francisco Syncope Rule (SFSR): admit pt if ≥1: ECG changes or non-sinus rhythm, dyspnea, Hct<30, SBP<90, HF
• Ddx: seizure, metabolic causes (hypoglycemia, hypoxia), intoxication/meds, vertebrobasilar TIA, fall, psychiatric, autonomic failure

panels.title: ETIOLOGY AND DIAGNOSIS: (AHA/ACC/HRS: JACC 2017;70:e39)
panels.text:
ETIOLOGY AND DIAGNOSIS: (AHA/ACC/HRS: JACC 2017;70:e39)
Etiology Historical Features Diagnosis Treatment

Cardiology Syncope
OVERVIEW
• Definition: transient (self-limited) loss of consciousness due to cerebral hypoperfusion that is associated with loss of postural tone,
followed by complete spontaneous recovery; excludes metabolic causes (e.g. hypoglycemia, hypoxia, intoxication)

o High-risk symptoms: preceding palpitations, exertional syncope, bleeding, syncope while supine, lack of prodrome, trauma

topics.title: Peripheral Artery Disease

panels.title: OVERVIEW (2024 GUIDELINE)
panels.text:
OVERVIEW (2024 GUIDELINE)
• Definition: arterial stenosis or occlusion causing an imbalance of blood flow relative to muscular metabolism (legs > arms)
• Epidemiology: smoking, DM, HTN, HLD, age (20% prevalence >70y), CKD, microvascular disease (Lancet 2013;382:1329)

panels.title: CLINICAL PRESENTATION AND DIAGNOSIS
panels.text:
CLINICAL PRESENTATION AND DIAGNOSIS
• Symptoms: (Circ 2006;113:e463)
o Classic claudication (10-35%) - reproducible exertional pain (buttock, thigh, calf, ankle), relieved by rest (differentiate from
pseudo-claudication from spinal stenosis); atypical leg pain (most common, 40-50%); asymptomatic (20-50%).
o Threatened limb (1-2%): pain at rest (improved w/ hanging feet off bed or walking), ulcers at pressure points, dry gangrene
o Rutherford classification: clinical criteria +/- objective data from treadmill test and ankle BP (JVascSurg;1997;26:517)
• Exam: arterial bruit, peripheral pulses (palpation, Doppler), cap refill, pallor on elevation, ulcers, atrophic changes, hair
• Diagnostics:
o ABI: Doppler US. Ratio of DP/PT (higher value) SBP to brachial SBP.
▪ Abnormal: ≤0.9 (95% Sn and 100% Sp for detecting arteriogram-positive lesions with ≥50% stenosis). ABI ≥1.40
suggests compressibility usually due to calcifications (e.g., elderly, DM, ESRD)
▪ If ABI ≥1.40, a toe brachial index can be used for diagnosis
o If ABI abnormal: obtain segmental ABI with pulse volume recordings (PVR) to localize disease
o Exercise testing: if high suspicion for PAD & normal resting ABIs
o If considering endovascular or surgical revascularization: Duplex US, CTA (with distal run off), MRA, or angiography
o Concern for chronic limb-threatening ischemia: skin perfusion pressure and transcutaneous oxygen pressure
ABI Interpretation Rutherford Rutherford Clinical Description
>1.40 Noncompressible vessel (not interpretable). Grade Stage
Due to extra-luminal vessel calcification 0 0 Asymptomatic
1.00 - 1.40 Normal 1 Mild claudication
0.91 - 0.99 Borderline I 2 Moderate claudication
0.41 - 0.90 Mild to moderate PAD 3 Severe claudication
0.00 - 0.40 Severe PAD II 4 Rest Pain
III 5 Minor tissue loss
6 Major tissue loss

panels.title: TREATMENT
panels.text:
TREATMENT
• Optimize CV risk factors (e.g., HTN, DM, HLD, weight loss), high-intensity statin, smoking cessation
• Formal exercise program
o CLEVER-RCT: supervised exercise therapy is at least as effective as stenting (JACC 2015;12:2055)
o ERASE-RCT: supervised exercise therapy + revascularization > exercise alone (JAMA 2015;314:1936)
• Anti-platelets: For secondary prevention. If symptomatic, ASA 75-162mg qd or clopidogrel 75mg qd: MI, CVA, vascular death
(NEJM 2017;376:32).If asymptomatic, consider ASA 81mg. Avoid DAPT (NEJM 2006;354:1706) unless clinically indicated, usually post-
revascularization for 1-6 months. Review w/ clinical decision making algorithm (JACC 2018;71:2450).
• Anti-coagulation: rivaroxaban 2.5mg BID + ASA if symptomatic or after revascularization: major adverse cardiac & limb events vs
ASA alone (Lancet 2018;391:219). Caution as major bleeding, but no fatal bleeding in pts w/ stable PAD in study
• Cilostazol: Start 100mg BID. PDE3 inhibitor w/ vasodilatory and anti-platelet effects. Adjunct for symptom relief refractory to exercise
therapy/smoking cessation. Use in combination with ASA or anti platelet (Chest 2012; 142:1608). Only AHA/ACC recommended med
to exercise capacity (Circ 2017;135:e686). Contraindicated in HF.
• Revascularization (endovascular, surgical, or hybrid): If threatened limb and/or severe symptoms refractory to medical management.
Choice of endovascular versus surgical repair depends on patient factors and anatomy (NEJM 2022;387:2305)
• Ulcers/footcare: surveillance by clinicians and patients; wound care and pressure offloading to promote healing, may need
revascularization for appropriate healing; amputation if no revascularization strategy. Use WIfI (J Vasc Surg 2013; 59:220) and
GLASS classification tools to guide revascularization vs amputation.

panels.title: ACUTE LIMB ISCHEMIA (BMJ 2000;320:764)
panels.text:
ACUTE LIMB ISCHEMIA (BMJ 2000;320:764)
• Sudden decrease (<2 wk) in limb perfusion threatening viability. Emergency – STAT consult Vascular Surgery and Vascular Medicine
o Viable: no immediate threat of tissue loss; audible arterial and venous Doppler signal, intact motor/sensory (category I)
o Threatened: salvage requires prompt intervention; inaudible arterial Doppler signal, audible venous Doppler signal, motor or
sensory deficits (category II)
o Irreversible: inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signal, complete loss of motor function and sensation (category III)
• Etiologies: embolic (e.g., AF, endocarditis) > thrombosis (e.g., atherosclerosis, APLAS, HIT), trauma, connective tissue disease
• Precipitating factors: dehydration, HoTN, abnormal posture (i.e. kneeling), malignancy, hyperviscosity, hypercoagulability
• Presentation: (6Ps) Pain, Poikilothermia, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia (unable to sense light touch), Paralysis
• Diagnosis: pulse (w/ Doppler) + neuro checks; angiography (CTA w/ run-off or arteriography)
• Treatment: anti-coagulation (UFH) ± IA lytic; endovascular or surgical repair vs thrombectomy if viable or threatened (category I and
II); may require prophylactic fasciotomy if threatened (category II); amputation if irreversible (category III)
• After treatment, monitor for reperfusion acidosis, hyper-K, rhabdomyolysis, & compartment syndrome

topics.text:
Cardiology Peripheral Artery Disease
OVERVIEW (2024 GUIDELINE)
• Definition: arterial stenosis or occlusion causing an imbalance of blood flow relative to muscular metabolism (legs > arms)
• Epidemiology: smoking, DM, HTN, HLD, age (20% prevalence >70y), CKD, microvascular disease (Lancet 2013;382:1329)
CLINICAL PRESENTATION AND DIAGNOSIS
• Symptoms: (Circ 2006;113:e463)
o Classic claudication (10-35%) - reproducible exertional pain (buttock, thigh, calf, ankle), relieved by rest (differentiate from
pseudo-claudication from spinal stenosis); atypical leg pain (most common, 40-50%); asymptomatic (20-50%).
o Threatened limb (1-2%): pain at rest (improved w/ hanging feet off bed or walking), ulcers at pressure points, dry gangrene
o Rutherford classification: clinical criteria +/- objective data from treadmill test and ankle BP (JVascSurg;1997;26:517)
• Exam: arterial bruit, peripheral pulses (palpation, Doppler), cap refill, pallor on elevation, ulcers, atrophic changes, hair
• Diagnostics:
o ABI: Doppler US. Ratio of DP/PT (higher value) SBP to brachial SBP.
▪ Abnormal: ≤0.9 (95% Sn and 100% Sp for detecting arteriogram-positive lesions with ≥50% stenosis). ABI ≥1.40
suggests compressibility usually due to calcifications (e.g., elderly, DM, ESRD)
▪ If ABI ≥1.40, a toe brachial index can be used for diagnosis
o If ABI abnormal: obtain segmental ABI with pulse volume recordings (PVR) to localize disease
o Exercise testing: if high suspicion for PAD & normal resting ABIs
o If considering endovascular or surgical revascularization: Duplex US, CTA (with distal run off), MRA, or angiography
o Concern for chronic limb-threatening ischemia: skin perfusion pressure and transcutaneous oxygen pressure
ABI Interpretation Rutherford Rutherford Clinical Description
>1.40 Noncompressible vessel (not interpretable). Grade Stage
Due to extra-luminal vessel calcification 0 0 Asymptomatic
1.00 - 1.40 Normal 1 Mild claudication
0.91 - 0.99 Borderline I 2 Moderate claudication
0.41 - 0.90 Mild to moderate PAD 3 Severe claudication
0.00 - 0.40 Severe PAD II 4 Rest Pain
III 5 Minor tissue loss
6 Major tissue loss
TREATMENT
• Optimize CV risk factors (e.g., HTN, DM, HLD, weight loss), high-intensity statin, smoking cessation
• Formal exercise program
o CLEVER-RCT: supervised exercise therapy is at least as effective as stenting (JACC 2015;12:2055)
o ERASE-RCT: supervised exercise therapy + revascularization > exercise alone (JAMA 2015;314:1936)
• Anti-platelets: For secondary prevention. If symptomatic, ASA 75-162mg qd or clopidogrel 75mg qd: MI, CVA, vascular death
(NEJM 2017;376:32).If asymptomatic, consider ASA 81mg. Avoid DAPT (NEJM 2006;354:1706) unless clinically indicated, usually post-
revascularization for 1-6 months. Review w/ clinical decision making algorithm (JACC 2018;71:2450).
• Anti-coagulation: rivaroxaban 2.5mg BID + ASA if symptomatic or after revascularization: major adverse cardiac & limb events vs
ASA alone (Lancet 2018;391:219). Caution as major bleeding, but no fatal bleeding in pts w/ stable PAD in study
• Cilostazol: Start 100mg BID. PDE3 inhibitor w/ vasodilatory and anti-platelet effects. Adjunct for symptom relief refractory to exercise
therapy/smoking cessation. Use in combination with ASA or anti platelet (Chest 2012; 142:1608). Only AHA/ACC recommended med
to exercise capacity (Circ 2017;135:e686). Contraindicated in HF.
• Revascularization (endovascular, surgical, or hybrid): If threatened limb and/or severe symptoms refractory to medical management.
Choice of endovascular versus surgical repair depends on patient factors and anatomy (NEJM 2022;387:2305)
• Ulcers/footcare: surveillance by clinicians and patients; wound care and pressure offloading to promote healing, may need
revascularization for appropriate healing; amputation if no revascularization strategy. Use WIfI (J Vasc Surg 2013; 59:220) and
GLASS classification tools to guide revascularization vs amputation.
ACUTE LIMB ISCHEMIA (BMJ 2000;320:764)
• Sudden decrease (<2 wk) in limb perfusion threatening viability. Emergency – STAT consult Vascular Surgery and Vascular Medicine
o Viable: no immediate threat of tissue loss; audible arterial and venous Doppler signal, intact motor/sensory (category I)
o Threatened: salvage requires prompt intervention; inaudible arterial Doppler signal, audible venous Doppler signal, motor or
sensory deficits (category II)
o Irreversible: inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signal, complete loss of motor function and sensation (category III)
• Etiologies: embolic (e.g., AF, endocarditis) > thrombosis (e.g., atherosclerosis, APLAS, HIT), trauma, connective tissue disease
• Precipitating factors: dehydration, HoTN, abnormal posture (i.e. kneeling), malignancy, hyperviscosity, hypercoagulability
• Presentation: (6Ps) Pain, Poikilothermia, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia (unable to sense light touch), Paralysis
• Diagnosis: pulse (w/ Doppler) + neuro checks; angiography (CTA w/ run-off or arteriography)
• Treatment: anti-coagulation (UFH) ± IA lytic; endovascular or surgical repair vs thrombectomy if viable or threatened (category I and
II); may require prophylactic fasciotomy if threatened (category II); amputation if irreversible (category III)
• After treatment, monitor for reperfusion acidosis, hyper-K, rhabdomyolysis, & compartment syndrome
Daniel Restifo

panels.title: JVP MEASUREMENT PEARLS(NEJM 2020;383:e132)
panels.text:
JVP MEASUREMENT PEARLS(NEJM 2020;383:e132)
EJV is a good proxy for IJV in most patients; good reliability
for discriminating high from low CVP (Chest 2011;139:95)
Distance from sternal angle to right atrium is variable
between patients and across positions (JGIM 2002;17:852
median 5 cm at 0, 8 cm at 30, 10 cm at 60); interpret JVP
in clinical context and trend while intervening on volume
status (McGee 2021)
Sonographic JVP when bedside JVP difficult to visualize;
correlates well with right atrial pressure (Ann Intern Med
2022;175:344, JASE 2023;36:278). Lay patient 30 - 45, scan with vascular probe in short-axis just above the clavicle to find IJV and CA
and slide cranially to find the IJV meniscus, then usual JVP calculation. Alternatively, if the IJV is distended (> carotid) with minimal
pulsation just above the clavicle at 45, can call JVD (JASE 2023;36:278). Easy rules: if IJ > carotid in short axis at 90°, rules in elevated
RAP. If IJ < carotid in short axis at 30°, rules out elevated RAP

panels.title: CARDIAC TELEMETRY: “RUNNING THE TELE”
panels.text:
CARDIAC TELEMETRY: “RUNNING THE TELE”
Step 1: Locate the name of the desired patient on the telemetry monitor and select their telemetry strip.
Step 2: Once on patient’s telemetry strip, select “Patient Data.”
Step 3: Click “Event Review” which will show you any abnormal events the patient had since being placed on telemetry. From this list,
click the desired episode of choice.
Step 4: After clicking on the desired event, you will have multiple options to choose from:
o Events: events sorted in reverse chronological order (e.g. runs of NSVT, bradycardia)
o FD Strip: telemetry strip for a specific moment in time
o FD Page: global view useful in identifying abrupt changes that can be zoomed in on using the FD Strip view
o Graphic Trends: graphic view of HR trends over time (e.g. abrupt HR jump from sinus into AVNRT)
o Calipers: interactive calipers used to calculate intervals on telemetry strip
While a patient is on telemetry, review indication daily and discontinue if not using monitoring for clinical decision-making (see Monitoring
and Prophylaxis page)
Saaket Agrawal

panels.title: TREATMENT
panels.text:
TREATMENT
• Supplemental oxygen therapy (see Oxygen Delivery Therapies for more detail):
o
NC: for every liter increase in O2, approx. ↑FiO2 0.03/L (max: 6L = 0.40 FiO2, dependent on Ve/entrainment)
o
NRB: can give FiO2 ~0.90, but in tachypneic patients, FiO2 ~0.60 (due to entrainment of room air)
o
HFNC: FiO2 0.6 to 1.0 at 10-60 L/min (humidified air); ↓90d mortality vs NIPPV for pts with hypoxemic respiratory failure not due
to cardiogenic pulmonary edema or obstructive lung disease (NEJM 2015;372:2185)
• NIPPV (BiPAP for COPD; CPAP for CHF): RR >25-30, accessory muscle use, pH <7.35, PaCO2 >45mmHg
• Intubation: see red flags above

panels.title: DISEASE SPECIFIC TREATMENT
panels.text:
DISEASE SPECIFIC TREATMENT
• CHF: CPAP, IV diuresis, nitrates (paste or drip, if BP room)
• Asthma: nebulizers (albuterol 2.5-5mg q20min or stacked DuoNeb), steroids (IV methylpred 125mg q6h), Mg (2g/20 min). Trial
BiPAP; however, if RR remains >25, VBG w/ nl or rising CO2, AMS, or bradycardia, discuss intubation. Decreasing wheeze can
portend respiratory collapse (sign of worsening air movement/increased bronchoconstriction).
• COPD: BiPAP, stacked DuoNebs, steroids (IV methylpred 60-125mg); abx if 2/3: #sputum volume, purulence, dyspnea
• Hemoptysis (massive): place pt in lateral decub, bleeding lung side DOWN; volume resuscitate, reverse coagulopathies, call IP and
.
• Mucus plugging: airway suctioning, percussion/chest PT, guaifenesin, place pt in lateral decubitus, good lung side down
• PE (see VTE Treatment); if high suspicion and no contraindication, start empiric AC (LMWH therapeutic faster vs UFH gtt). Consult
• PTX: if unstable, bedside needle thoracostomy (STAT page Thoracic Surgery, 14G angiocath, 5th intercostal space at mid-axillary
line or 2nd intercostal space at mid-clavicular line); then chest tube (Thoracic Surgery or IP)
• Pleural effusion: Consult IP for thoracentesis (see Thoracentesis )
• Opioid overdose: Narcan 0.4-2mg IV/IM q2min, observe response, up titrate to adequate RR. Given short half-life, consider gtt if
responsive to bolus at 2/3 of bolus dose per hour (ex: 0.2–0.6 mg/h)
• Anaphylaxis: Initial: epi (1:1000) 0.3mL = 0.3mg IM, q5-15min PRN. Other agents may follow: diphenhydramine 25-
50mg IV, nebulized albuterol, methylprednisolone 1-2mg/kg IV, if persistent may require epi gtt.
• ACS (see ACS): ASA 325mg, atorvastatin 80mg, nitrates (SL/nitro paste/nitro gtt), heparin, consult Cardiology
Lauren Nguyen

panels.text:
HYPOXEMIC RESPIRATORY FAILURE
• Hypoventilation & low FiO2: decreased O2 delivery to lungs
• V/Q mismatch: imbalance in delivery of oxygenated air & blood flow (JAP 1964;19:713)
↑ pulmonary vasoconstriction can ↓hypoxemia by ↓Q to poorly
o
ventilated regions to ↑V/Q matching (ratio closer to 1)
1. FOCAL alveolar infiltrates: pus (PNA), edema, hemorrhage (DAH),
cells (cancer), aspiration, lipids/protein (PAP)
2. Airway: asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis
3. Vascular: pHTN, PE
• Shunt: flow of blood through lung without encountering oxygenated
air, “perfusion without ventilation” (severe V/Q mismatch). Will not improve with
supplemental oxygen (refractory hypoxemia)
1. DIFFUSE alveolar infiltrates: above + ARDS
2. Alveolar collapse: PTX, atelectasis, mucus plug
3. Intra-cardiac/pulm shunts: PFO/ASD/VSD (↑PEEP worsens this by ↑west
zones 1&2 = ↑RV afterload), AVM (e.g., hepatopulmonary syndrome)
• Impaired diffusion (↓DLCO): hypoxemia worse w/ exertion,
ILD (correlates with severity on CT), pHTN, advanced COPD

panels.title: HYPERCAPNIC RESPIRATORY FAILURE
panels.text:
HYPERCAPNIC RESPIRATORY FAILURE
• “Won’t breathe” (↓RR): sedatives, obesity hypoventilation, brainstem
stroke/tumor/infection, central sleep apnea, compensation for metabolic alkalosis ACID-BASE INTERPRETATION
(chemoreceptors), myxedema coma Hypercapnia→ Resp acidosis (↑pCO2)
• “Can’t breathe” (↓VA): •Acute: HCO3 ↑ by 1 (per pCO2 ↑ 10)
1. ↑ Dead space: airspace not participating in gas exchange; “V without Q” •Chronic: HCO3 ↑ by 3-4 (per pCO2 ↑ 10)
 Anatomic: (~150cc upper airway air without perfusion) + alveolar (AKA Hypocapnia→ Resp alkalosis (↓pCO2)
West Zone 1) ~0 normally; in disease, capillaries get destroyed or •Acute: HCO3 ↓ by 2 (per pCO2 ↓ 10)
compressed → ↑VD •Chronic: HCO3 ↓ by 5 (per pCO2 ↓ 10)
 Parenchyma: emphysema, ILD/fibrosis, HF, PNA, ARDS
 Airway: asthma/COPD, CF, bronchiectasis, OSA, tumor, high PEEP
 Vascular: severe PE → wasted V due to blocked Q
2. Chest wall/pleural constraints → ↓ lung volume: effusion/fibrosis, obesity, kyphosis/scoliosis, abd distension, PTX
3. Neuromuscular (Neurol Clin 2012;30:161): most apparent if unable to augment ventilation (eg in ALS: more often see ↓pCO2
secondary to hyperventilation); trend at bedside with single breath test (non-intubated pts) or negative inspiratory force (NIF)
(intubated pts). Consider EMG.
 Ddx: neuropathy (C-spine/phrenic nerve, GBS, ALS, polio), NMJ disorder (MG, botulism), myopathy
(polymyositis/dermatomyositis, hypophosphatemia), critical illness
• ↑CO2 production (VCO2): ↑WOB, fever, seizure, sepsis, steroids, overfeeding, thyrotoxicosis

panels.title: HIGH FLOW NASAL CANNULA (HFNC) & NONINVASIVE POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION (NIPPV) NEJM 2022;387:1688-98
panels.text:
HIGH FLOW NASAL CANNULA (HFNC) & NONINVASIVE POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION (NIPPV) NEJM 2022;387:1688-98
HFNC NIPPV (CPAP + BiPAP)
Parameters Flow: 10-60 LPM (up to 80 LPM at some institutions) CPAP: constant level of pos. pressure; targets oxygenation
FiO2 (%): 21-100 BLPAP (or BiPAP™): provides positive inspiratory pressure
PEEP generated with a closed mouth is about 1 cm of water (IPAP) above PEEP with each pt-triggered breath; targets
pressure for 10L flow ventilation and oxygenation
Physiologic Effects Oxygenation: ↑ delivery of O2, some PEEP Oxygenation: ↓atelectasis, ↓upper airway obstruction,
Ventilation: ↑ventilation (↓dead space during expiration) ↓WOB (& O2 consumption)
Other: Humidification ↑mucociliary clearance of secretions Ventilation: ↑tidal volume and minute ventilation (via IPAP)
Other: ↓venous return (↓LV & RV preload), ↓LV afterload
Clinical Scenarios
Acute hypoxemic -Mixed evidence for HFNC in NON-hypercapnic resp. failure. NIPPV may ↓mortality & ↓intubation (JAMA 2020;324:57).
respiratory failure May ↓intubation, but no Δ in mortality or LOS vs standard O2 -Consider if also significant hypercapnia, e.g. OHS,
(AHRF) tx (Cochrane 2020). neuromuscular failure (e.g. ALS, MG).
-Consider HF 1st if ILD, ARDS physio, and may be non-inf to Caveats: (AJRCCM 2017;195:67-77)
BIPAP in PNA. Can be used as rescue in asthma or in pts -P:F < 150: ↑ death vs. up-front intubation
that can’t tolerate BiPAP to help w/ dead space wash and -TV > 9-9.5 cc/kg IDW: ↑death, ↑intubation
intubation eval
Acute COPD Strong indication for BiPAP (ERS/ATS: ERJ 2017;50) to off-load respiratory muscles, counteract dynamic hyperinflation,
exacerbation w ↑ventilation a ↓mortality, ↓intubation, & ↓ LOS (Cochrane Rev 2017). Asthma can be treated similarly but there is less
resp. acidosis evidence to support.
Acute cardiogenic NIPPV (BiPAP / CPAP) ↓intubation, ↓in-hospital mortality by ↓ WOB, ↑FRC, ↓LV / RV preload, ↓LV afterload (NEJM
pulmonary edema 2008;359:142; Cochrane Rev 2013)
Post-extubation Extub. to NIPPV or HFNC to ↓ reintubation and post-extub. resp. failure in ↑risk pts: COPD, obesity (JAMA 2016;316:1565)
Contraindications to NIPPV:
• Risk of delay: emergent indication for intubation, acute life-threatening non-respiratory organ failure
• Risk of aspiration (d/t gastric insufflation): cannot clear secretions, AMS if pt cannot remove mask (exception: AMS due to
hypercapnia)
• Risk of injury: PTX (can induce tension physiology), recent esophageal anastomosis or tear, cannot tolerate ↓preload from ↓venous
return, recent facial trauma/surgery

• Risk of failure varies based on cause (15-20% COPD exacerbations, 40-60% AHRF) and ↑ with severity of respiratory failure
• ROX index: tool for prediction of HFNC failure & monitoring for need for intubation in pts with pneumonia (AJRCCM 2019;199:1468-
76)
• HACOR score: tool for prediction of NIPPV failure & need for intubation (ICU Med 2017;43:192-9)
• Sedation: IV Precedex, Haldol, and Zyprexa can be considered to help pts tolerate NIPPV w/o suppressing resp drive (see sedation)

consider ABG/VBG to assess oxygenation/ventilation. If no improvement, discuss escalation of care to ICU
REMEMBER: BiPAP/HFNC MUST NOT DELAY AN INDICATED INTUBATION!

topics.title: Interpretation of Chest Imaging

panels.title: CHEST X-RAY
panels.text:
CHEST X-RAY
Systematic approach to CXR (ABCDEF approach):
1. (A)ssess technical quality and (A)irways:
• Rotation: ensure spinous processes bisect btwn medial end of clavicles
• Lung volumes: adequate inspiratory effort is 9-10 posterior ribs
• Penetration: good when vertebral bodies visible behind cardiac silhouette
• Airways: look for narrowing, deviation, foreign bodies. ITP pushes
trachea away (PTX). ITP pulls trachea towards (atelectasis/plugging).
• (A)lways compare previous studies.
2. (B)ones/soft tissue: subcutaneous air, rib fractures, cervical ribs
3. (C)ardiac Silhouette (mediastinum/hilum): AP films  cardiac silhouette. CT
ratio=max cardiac width/max thoracic width, >50% suggests cardiomegaly
(only PA films). Widened mediastinum generally >8cm (watch out for rotation).
4. (D)iaphragm (gastric bubble): left hemidiaphragm is usually lower than
right. Flattening of diaphragm sensitive for emphysema.
5. (E)ffusions: blunting of CP angle. Small effusions seen 1st on PA lateral.
Fluid not seen on upright chest until >250ml.  sensitivity when semi
recumbent or supine. Can assess free flowing vs. loculated effusions on lateral decubitus view (free flowing will track equality on horizontal
plane vs. loculated will not).
6. (F)ields (lung fields) & (F)oreign bodies (lines/drains): Look for focal vs. diffuse processes PTX, PNA, pulm edema. Look for silhouette
sign (loss of the normal visible border of an intrathoracic structure) that indicates pulmonary density. Look for lines/tubes (see
Interpretation of Common Studies). ETT ideally 3-5cm from carina, adjust if not.

panels.title: CT CHEST
panels.text:
CT CHEST
• To characterize abnormal CXR w/ cross-section or w/ suspicion for
pathology despite unrevealing CXR
• HRCT (thin-section CT, <2mm): for diagnosing diffuse lung path. Must
be non-con. Includes expiratory, inspiratory, prone and supine images.
Approach to interpretation:
• Review scout imaging: gives anatomic overview.
• Review lines/tubes, extra-thoracic abnormalities.
• Mediastinum/Heart/Vessels: soft tissue window: LV>RV normally.
Diameter of main PA should be < ascending aorta (PA >= 29 mm: PPV
97% for pHTN, Pulm HTN radiology). Cor calcium visible on non-con.
• Airways: review in soft tissue and lung windows. Inspiratory HRCT=
round trachea; Expiratory HRCT= “D-shaped” trachea.
Common Findings Definition Associated Etiologies
Consolidations Complete filling of alveoli, dense ↑ attenuation obscuring underlying lung PNA > Malignancy
architecture +/- air bronchograms
GGOs Partial filling of alveoli +/- interstitium, appears as hazy ↑ lung attenuation Infxn, edema, blood, fibrosis,
(light gray) that does NOT obscure underlying architecture malignancy
Tree-in-Bud Branching linear opacities & nodules that represent dz’d lobular bronchioles Infxn (incl. TB), CTD, ABPA,
(AJR 2009; 193:472) or bronchiolitis & filling with fluid, pus, mucus, or tumor emboli malignancy, endarteritis, CF
Emphysema Airspace enlargement > 1-2 cm in diameter. “Bleb” = similar, but < 1-2 cm COPD, congenital, spontaneous
Mosaic Attenuation Patchy ↓ and ↑attenuation areas due to air trapping, decreased perfusion, HP, obstruction, CTEPH, Infxn,
GGOs. Air trapping identified as worsening with expiratory films. Edema/hemorrhage
Honeycombing Clustering of cystic airspace disease. Microcystic <4mm, macrocystic >4mm ILD: NSIP <4mm; IPF>4mm
Subpleural Retic. Linear opacification of the inter/intralobar septae around 1 cm from pleura. UIP>NSIP, normal w/ aging
Atelectasis, Effusion Atelectasis enhances w/ con, resolves proned. Effusion more homogeneous
Consolidations GGOs Tree-in-bud opacities Centrilobular Nodules Emphysema Atelectasis & Eff.
Mosaic Attenuation Honeycombing Subpleural Reticulation ILS Thickening Bronchiectasis
Madison Masters

panels.text:
ASTHMA(GINA 2024, NAEPP 2020) *note: dx criteria currently vary between societies (e.g., ATS vs GINA)
Definition: heterogeneous condition with resp sx (wheeze, SOB, chest tightness, cough) and variable expiratory airflow limitation
Symptoms Resp sx (wheeze, SOB, cough, chest tightness) that vary over time & intensity, worse @ night/early AM
Triggers Exercise, cold air, allergens, irritants (e.g., smoke), viral respiratory infections, drugs (ASA, NSAIDS, β-blockers)
Diagnosis: (+) Bronchodilator response (↑FEV1 or FVC ≥12% & >200mL or PEF (*if no spirometry avail) ≥20%), improvement
Spirometry/peak w/ ICS x4wks (↑FEV1 ≥12% & >200mL or PEF ≥20%), variability in BID PEF x 2wks (avg variability >10%),
expiratory flow (PEF) w orsens w/ methacholine (FEV1 ↓≥20%), high variability between visits (FEV1 ≥12% & >200mL or PEF ≥20%)
Inflammatory Type 2 inflammation high (↑eos, ↑FeNO, ↑IgE, atopy; consider biologics in severe asthma) T2-low (increased
phenotype neutrophils, often steroid-refractory)
New-onset adult cases ddx: systemic disease (ABPA, EGPA, systemic mastocytosis), occupational asthma (10-25%; NEJM 2014;370:640),
ASA-exacerbated resp. disease (7%, esp. if nasal polyps; J Allergy Clin Immunol 2015;135:676)

panels.title: ASTHMA EXACERBATIONS
panels.text:
ASTHMA EXACERBATIONS
OUTPATIENT: short course pred. 40-50mg x5-7d + controller/reliever regimen, consider 4x controller ICS if mild (NEJM 2018;278:902)
INPATIENT: assess severity of exacerbation (VS, mental status, SpO2, WOB, PEF <50%), consider VBG/ABG if severe
Severe: ↑resp drive→↑RR→↓pCO2, nl/↓pH suggest resp. failure. If sig hypoxemia, consider resp. failure vs PTX, PNA, PE, plug, etc.
Floor Patient ICU Patient (Thorax 2003;58:81; J Clin Med 2019)
- Bronchodilators: albuterol (2.5-5g) ± ipratropium (0.5-1.5mg) - Bronchodilators: albuterol + ipratropium, Methylpred 125mg IV q6h
q20m x3 - NIV: short trial, typically BiPAP
DuoNebs in ED a/w admit (Cochrane Rev 2017) - Rescue therapies: Mg IV 2g, continuous albuterol (CAB). Less data:
o
IV β-agonist, ketamine, inhaled anesthetic, Heliox. ECMO=last resort
- Steroids: pred 40-60mg total x5-7d (Cochrane Rev 2016)
- Mechanical ventilation: large ETT (8+), ↑insp flow rate (80-
- O2 93-95%; >95% increases pCO2; Thorax 2011;66:937)
100L/min), ↓VT (6-8cc/kg), ↓RR (10-14), ↓PEEP, paralysis; Goal:
- If impending respiratory failure: stacked DuoNebs (x3/h),
max exp. phase, minimize hyperinflation, permissive hypercapnia
methylpred IV 60-125mg q6h, Mg IV 2g/20min, transfer to ICU

Symptoms Resp sx (wheeze, SOB, cough, chest tightness) that vary over time & intensity, worse @ night/early AM
Triggers Exercise, cold air, allergens, irritants (e.g., smoke), viral respiratory infections, drugs (ASA, NSAIDS, β-blockers)

expiratory flow (PEF) w orsens w/ methacholine (FEV1 ↓≥20%), high variability between visits (FEV1 ≥12% & >200mL or PEF ≥20%)
Inflammatory Type 2 inflammation high (↑eos, ↑FeNO, ↑IgE, atopy; consider biologics in severe asthma) T2-low (increased
phenotype neutrophils, often steroid-refractory)
New-onset adult cases ddx: systemic disease (ABPA, EGPA, systemic mastocytosis), occupational asthma (10-25%; NEJM 2014;370:640),
ASA-exacerbated resp. disease (7%, esp. if nasal polyps; J Allergy Clin Immunol 2015;135:676)

panels.title: Source content

DEFINITION: persistent respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough, sputum production, recurrent wheezing, exacerbations) d/t abnormalities of airways
(bronchitis, bronchiolitis) and/or alveoli (emphysema) that lead to persistent airflow obstruction (GOLD 2025)

panels.title: DIAGNOSIS AND STAGING (GOLD 2025: AJRCCM 2017;195:557)
panels.text:
DIAGNOSIS AND STAGING (GOLD 2025: AJRCCM 2017;195:557)
1.Diagnosis: respiratory sx + fixed obstruction w/ FEV1/FVC <0.7 or <LLN on spirometry post-bronchodilator
2.GOLD Grade (1-4) is defined by severity of airflow limitation (FEV1% of predicted); helps establish prognosis
& guide non-medical therapy
3.GOLD Group (“ABE”) is defined by exacerbations &
sx guide therapy (mMRC, CAT score)
4.Other testing: lung volumes, DLCO (<60% a/w sx,
exercise, ↓health), exercise test (6MWT), α1-antitrypsin

panels.title: DIFFERENTIAL
panels.text:
DIFFERENTIAL
Pre-COPD: respiratory symptoms with structural lung lesions (emphysema) and/or physiological abnormalities w/o airflow obstruction. Preserved Ratio Impaired
Spirometry (PRISm): respiratory sx w/ normal ratio (FEV1/FVC > 0.7) but impaired FEV1 (< 80) after bronchodilation. Chronic bronchitis: overlapping condition;
chronic cough + sputum > 3 months / yr for 2+ years. Asthma: see “PFTs and Asthma.” Bronchiectasis: large vol of purulent sputum, a/w bacterial infxn &
bronchial dilation on CXR/HRCT. Obliterative bronchiolitis: consider after lung/BM transplant, HRCT: hypodense areas on exp.
Diffuse pan-bronchiolitis: Asian pts, chronic sinusitis, CXR/HRCT: diffuse small centrilobular nodular opacities & hyperinflation

topics.title: Bronchiectasis & Hemoptysis

panels.title: BRONCHIECTASIS (NEJM 2022;387:533; RM 2020;166)
panels.text:
BRONCHIECTASIS (NEJM 2022;387:533; RM 2020;166)
Definition Permanent airway dilatation from recurrent infxn/inflammation
Symptoms Chronic productive cough, recurrent bronchitis/pneumonia, wheezing, dyspnea, hemoptysis, recurrent pleurisy
Recurrent insult: infection (PNA, MAC, TB, PsA, childhood infections, ABPA), inhalation, GERD/aspiration
Impaired immunity: ↓mucus clearance (CF, 1° ciliary dyskinesia [PCD]), immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV, CVID, ↓IgG)
Etiology
Obstruction: foreign body, tumor, COPD, tracheomalacia/tracheobronchomegaly, Marfan’s, radiation
Systemic disease: RA, Sjogren’s, SLE, IBD, A1AT; Idiopathic = ~50%
Dx: 1) productive cough most days/week, 2) exacerbations, and 3) CT w/ ≥1 of: bronchial diameter > adj artery (signet-ring
sign), thickened bronchi w/ lack of tapering (tram track sign), radiographically visible airways in perimeter
Workup Initial: High-resolution CT, PFTs, CBC/diff, Ig levels, sputum cx (bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal)
As indicated: CF eval (gene/sweat Cl- testing), Aspergillus IgE, ANA, RF/CCP, SSA/SSB, A1AT, HIV, Ig levels; consider
nasal NO (PCD), pneumococcal vaccine titers (often low), bronch w/BAL, colonoscopy (IBD), pH/motility testing
Natural Hx Exacerbations, ↓ in FEV1, PsA colonization → worsening disease; prog. w/ Bronchiectasis Severity Index or FACED

HEMOPTYSIS (Chest 2020;157:77; Am Fam Physician 2022;105:144)
Expectoration of blood from lower respiratory tract. Non-massive: if minimal (<30mL) & benign (eg.
infxn/bronchiectasis): observe. If active, recurrent, >1w: CT  bronch. MASSIVE HEMOPTYSIS (>500mL/d
Definition
or >100mL/h) = life-threatening emergency with mortality 50-80%. Asphyxiation, NOT exsanguination, is
mechanism of death (maximum pulmonary blood volume ~500mL)
• Airway: bronchitis, bronchiectasis (incl. CF), masses (usually 1* lung CA), trauma (incl. foreign body)
Etiology • Pulmonary parenchyma: infection (PNA, abscess, TB, aspergilloma), vasculitis (ANCA, anti-GBM, immune-
(common & life- complex, drug-induced; see Vasculitis and Autoantibodies), coagulopathy, endometriosis, inhalation injury,
threatening) collagen defect, sarcoid, pulmonary hemosiderosis, trauma

panels.text:
DIFFUSE ALVEOLAR HEMORRHAGE (Chest 2010;137:1164)
Presentation: hemoptysis (can be absent in 1/3), cough, fever, dyspnea, diffuse radiographic opacities, abnormal gas
exchange
Etiology: disruption of alveolar-capillary basement membrane from: capillaritis (rheum, drugs, idiopathic), bland hemorrhage
(AC, ↓plt, HF), or diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS, infxn, PE, drugs)
Workup: CXR, CT (diffuse GGO central > peripheral), BAL (serial washings show ↑blood), labs guided by clinical picture
Management: Primarily supportive. Manage hypoxemia and treat underlying etiology, eg.: Capillaritis/AI syndromes: Systemic
glucocorticoids (pulse dose IV methylpred 500-1000mg/d up to 5 doses w/ taper), cyclophosphamide, rituximab ±
plasmapheresis. Excess AC/bleeding disorder: reverse AC. (Int J Mol Sci. 2021;22:793)
